Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset répond aux Qurayshites qui réclamaient des signes semblables à ceux des prophètes antérieurs : le Coran lui-même est un signe permanent, récité à chaque époque et en tout lieu, source de miséricorde et de rappel pour ceux qui croient, c'est-à-dire pour ceux qui cherchent la vérité sans obstination. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Atiyya rattachent le verset aux Qurayshites, tandis qu'al-Qurtubi et al-Baydawi évoquent aussi la possibilité d'un sens concernant les Juifs, qui retrouvaient dans leurs livres les traits du Prophète. La plupart citent une tradition rapportée par Yahya ibn Ja'da au sujet de feuillets contenant des extraits de la Torah, que le Prophète aurait désapprouvés ; al-Tabari et Ibn 'Atiyya tiennent cette tradition à distance, Ibn 'Atiyya préférant le sens général. Al-Razi montre que le Coran est une preuve plus complète que les miracles passés, car il subsiste et il atteint tous les lieux, et que la miséricorde réside dans la distinction entre le véritable prophète et l'imposteur. Ibn Sa'di et al-Sha'rawi y voient une guérison des âmes et une guidance, réservées à ceux qui le reçoivent avec un cœur droit. Al-Zamakhshari fait de l'interrogation un reproche de ne pas se contenter du Coran, et Ibn 'Ashur énumère cinq qualités qui le distinguent des autres miracles. Tous s'accordent sur le fait que le témoignage de Dieu suffit, et que les véritables perdants sont ceux qui ont cru au faux et renié Dieu.

Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète ﷺ de dire aux païens qui réclamaient un miracle éclatant que Dieu suffit comme témoin entre lui et eux, Lui qui sait ce qui est dans les cieux et sur la terre, et qui connaît sa situation comme la leur. Les exégètes ont différemment compris ce témoignage. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Nasafi y voient le témoignage de Dieu en faveur de la véracité du Prophète, appuyé par les signes et par le Livre qu'Il a fait descendre ; al-Mawardi le comprend comme un témoignage de sincérité et de transmission, Dieu attestant aussi de leur déni. Le verset précédent, selon Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi ou Ibn Kathir, signifie que le Coran lui-même suffit comme miracle, car il est une preuve durable, récitée en tout temps et en tout lieu, une miséricorde et un rappel pour les croyants. Plusieurs rapportent à ce propos l'occasion de la révélation : des musulmans apportèrent au Prophète des écrits contenant des propos juifs, et il les rejeta ; ce récit est cité par al-Tabari, al-Mawardi et d'autres, sans qu'ils tranchent unanimement. Quant à l'expression « ceux qui croient au faux », la plupart y voient les idolâtres qui adorent d'autres que Dieu ; al-Tabari la rapporte à l'association, Yahya ibn Sallam à Iblis, Mouqatil au culte de Satan. Al-Razi montre que tout ce qui n'est pas Dieu est vain. Le verbe « perdre » désigne, selon al-Mawardi, la ruine de soi, et selon d'autres la perte du Jardin. Le tour employé adoucit le ton, comme le remarquent al-Zamakhshari et Abu al-Su'ud.

Dieu rapporte que les païens pressaient le Prophète ﷺ de leur envoyer le châtiment, par moquerie et par dénégation, comme le fit al-Nadr ibn al-Harith en disant : « Fais pleuvoir sur nous des pierres du ciel ». Dieu n'a pas hâté ce châtiment, car il a fixé pour lui un terme connu qui ne peut ni avancer ni reculer ; sans ce terme, le châtiment les aurait atteints aussitôt. Il affirme ensuite que le châtiment viendra sur eux soudainement, alors qu'ils sont inattentifs et ignorent le moment de sa venue. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur la cause de cette précipitation, qui est le défi et la raillerie, mais divergent sur le sens du terme fixé. Ibn Jubayr, al-Zamakhshari et Ibn Kathir y voient le Jour de la Résurrection ; al-Dahhak y voit la durée de leur vie ; Yahya ibn Sallam y voit le premier souffle de la trompe ; et beaucoup, dont Ibn 'Abbas et al-Nasafi, y voient le jour de Badr ou l'heure de leur mort à leur terme. Quant au châtiment qui vient soudainement, certains l'entendent comme le châtiment d'ici-bas, tel que la bataille de Badr, tandis qu'Ibn Jizzi et Ibn Kathir l'entendent comme le châtiment de l'au-delà. Ibn Kathir rapporte que Jahannam enveloppe les infidèles ; il cite aussi une interprétation, qu'il juge étrange, selon laquelle Jahannam serait la mer. Certains lecteurs lisent « yaqulu » et d'autres « naqulu », différence qui ne modifie guère le sens. Ibn 'Ashur considère ce verset comme une réponse à leurs objections, contenant une menace de deux châtiments, l'un proche et l'autre plus grave dans la Géhenne. Al-Sha'rawi souligne que les hommes ignorent le moment du châtiment qui viendra à son terme fixé.

Ce verset parle des incroyants qui pressaient le Prophète ﷺ de faire venir le châtiment dont il les menaçait, par moquerie et par défi. Selon les commentateurs, le châtiment les atteindra inévitablement, et la Géhenne les entoure déjà et les attend. Les exégètes s'accordent à dire que les « incroyants » désignés ici sont ceux-là mêmes qui réclament le châtiment, et que l'encerclement signifie qu'aucun d'eux n'échappera à la Géhenne. Ibn Kathir et d'autres y voient une annonce selon laquelle la Géhenne les rassemblera tous, sans exception. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi, eux, considèrent que l'encerclement peut être futur, ou bien présent, puisque la mécréance et les fautes qui la mènent les entourent déjà. Pour le « terme fixé » (ajal musammâ) mentionné juste avant, Ibn Abbas et Ibn Jubayr y voient le Jour de la Résurrection, Qatada la durée de la vie jusqu'à la mort puis jusqu'à la résurrection, Yahya ibn Sallam le premier souffle de la trompe, Al-Dahhak la durée de leur vie, et d'autres la bataille de Badr. Quant à la « Géhenne » elle-même, Ikrima l'interprète comme la mer, avis qu'Ibn Atiyya et Ibn Kathir jugent faible ou étrange, la plupart des commentateurs y voyant le feu connu. Les lectures diffèrent sur le verbe « il dira » (yaqulu), à la troisième personne ou à la première du pluriel, selon qu'on y entend Dieu, un ange chargé du châtiment ou une majesté divine. Ibn Kathir et al-Sa'di rattachent ce passage au châtiment de l'au-delà, auquel nul n'échappe, que le châtiment d'ici-bas leur soit hâté ou différé.

Ce verset décrit le jour du Jugement où le châtiment enveloppera les mécréants par-dessus eux et sous leurs pieds, tandis qu'il leur sera dit, en guise de reproche : goûtez ce que vous faisiez. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que la Géhenne les entoure et que le châtiment les atteint de toutes parts, ce qui en accroît la rigueur. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir expliquent que cette idée de recouvrement venant d'en haut et d'en bas signifie que le feu les cerne de tous côtés, Ibn Kathir la rapprochant d'autres versets sur les ombres de feu. Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Ashur voient dans la parole adressée aux damnés une humiliation morale qui s'ajoute au tourment physique. Le verset se rattache au contexte où les Quraychites réclamaient avec défi la venue du châtiment : al-Baghawi, al-Razi et al-Qurtubi rapportent que cette demande était une moquerie et un démenti, et qu'Allah avait différé le châtiment jusqu'à un terme fixé, dont les interprétations varient selon Ibn 'Abbas (le Jour de la Résurrection), Qatada (la durée de la vie et la mort), Dahhak (la durée de leur vie) ou le combat de Badr. Sur la lecture, Nafi' et les Kufiens lisent « yaqulu » à la troisième personne, tandis qu'Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Amir lisent « naqulu » à la première personne du pluriel, ce qui, selon al-Qurtubi et al-Alusi, renvoie à Allah ou à un ange chargé du châtiment. Al-Razi relève que le verset établit une gradation : le feu vient des côtés supérieurs, alors qu'il ne monte pas naturellement vers le haut en ce monde. Ibn 'Ashur note que l'omission des côtés droit et gauche sert à la concision dans un contexte de menace.

Dieu s'adresse à ses serviteurs croyants qui ne pouvaient plus l'adorer librement à La Mecque : Sa terre est vaste, et lorsqu'il est impossible de Le servir dans un pays, il faut émigrer vers un autre et Lui vouer seul son culte. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que le verset appelle à quitter une terre où la foi est persécutée ou empêchée, et beaucoup le rattachent aux croyants faibles de La Mecque, comme le rapportent Muqatil et al-Kalbi, puis Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn Kathir. Sa'id ibn Jubayr et 'Ata' estiment qu'il faut sortir de toute terre où le péché se répand sans qu'on puisse le changer, position que Malik rejoint selon Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Qurtubi. Mujahid y voit l'appel à émigrer et à combattre, Abu al-'Aliya l'appel à rechercher les amis de Dieu, tandis qu'Ibn Zayd comprend qu'il s'adresse aux croyants de La Mecque. Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir comprend au contraire que la vastesse concerne la miséricorde ou la subsistance divine. Al-Tabari retient l'exil comme sens le plus évident, car la suite « Me seul, adorez-Moi » le confirme. Les exégètes rappellent que la mort n'épargne personne, qu'il ne faut donc pas craindre de partir, et que Dieu pourvoit à la subsistance des émigrés comme à celle des animaux qui n'amassent rien. Le hadith cité par al-Baydawi et al-Nasafi, selon lequel celui qui fuit sa religion d'une terre à une autre, fût-ce d'un empan, mérite le Paradis, est rapporté par plusieurs d'entre eux. Quant à la syntaxe, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan et al-Alusi discutent du rôle de la fa' et de la mise en avant de l'objet, qu'ils lient à une condition sous-entendue.

Ce verset affirme que toute âme goûtera la mort, puis qu'elle sera ramenée vers Dieu. Les commentateurs le replacent dans le contexte de l'appel à émigrer hors d'une terre d'idolâtrie vers un lieu où l'on peut adorer Dieu : il rassure les croyants en leur rappelant que la mort atteint chacun, où qu'il se trouve. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn Kathir y voient le sens de l'émigration, tandis que Mujahid et Ibn Jubayr parlent de fuir les lieux de désobéissance. Selon Zamakhshari, Nasafi et Abu al-Su'ud, « goûter » la mort signifie en éprouver l'amertume et l'angoisse, et l'expression rejoint ainsi une image de la mort comme breuvage amer. Al-Razi propose une lecture plus subtile : celui qui se rattache à Dieu plutôt qu'à lui-même échappe à la véritable mort, qui est pour les croyants un simple passage. Al-Baydawi et Ibn 'Ashur insistent sur la dimension de jugement et de rétribution du retour vers Dieu. Sur le plan de la lecture, Ibn al-Jawzi et Abu Hayyan rapportent des variantes : « turji'un » se lit à la deuxième personne chez la majorité et à la troisième chez Abu Bakr selon Asim. Le hadith cité par Baghawi et Ibn Kathir, qui relie le verset à l'interdiction d'accumuler la nourriture, est jugé faible par Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir et Shawkani, parce qu'il contredit la pratique attestée du Prophète. Le message commun est que la mort est inéluctable, et qu'elle ne doit donc pas dissuader de l'obéissance.

Ce verset annonce que ceux qui croient et accomplissent les bonnes œuvres seront installés par Dieu dans des chambres élevées du Paradis, sous lesquelles coulent les rivières, où ils demeureront éternellement ; quelle excellente récompense pour ceux qui agissent bien. Les commentateurs rappellent que ce passage vient après l'appel adressé aux croyants faibles de La Mecque à émigrer, et qu'il les encourage par la promesse de cette récompense. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et al-Zamakhshari expliquent que le verbe « nubawwi'annahum » signifie « installer » et qu'une lecture avec la lettre thāʾ, « nathwiyannahum », signifie « faire demeurer » ; ils considèrent les deux lectures comme proches de sens. Les « ghuraf » désignent des demeures élevées. Tous insistent sur la patience et la confiance en Dieu comme l'essentiel du bien ; les patients sont ceux qui persévèrent dans la foi, l'émigration et la souffrance infligée par les polythéistes. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Jawzi notent que la subsistance n'est pas liée à un lieu précis : Dieu nourrit les animaux et ceux qui émigrent. Al-Razi remarque que l'absence de précision sur ce qui se trouve au-dessus des chambres marque leur haute élévation, contrairement au châtiment des incroyants, dont le feu est dit au-dessus d'eux. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Qurtubi rapportent que « Ma terre est vaste » peut signifier : émigrez d'une terre d'injustice, ou que la miséricorde et la subsistance de Dieu sont vastes, ou encore qu'il faut lutter contre les ennemis de Dieu. Tous rappellent que la mort atteint chacun, ce qui ne doit pas détourner le croyant de l'obéissance. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi et al-Shawkani jugent faibles certains récits sur la cause de la révélation du verset sur l'animal qui n'emporte pas sa subsistance, mais retiennent le sens commun : les bêtes ne thésaurisent pas, et Dieu pourvoit à leur subsistance.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset (29:59) conclut la description de ceux qui ont cru et accompli les bonnes œuvres : ce sont « ceux qui ont patienté » face aux épreuves, à l'hostilité des polythéistes et à l'exil, et qui « placent leur confiance en leur Seigneur », c'est-à-dire s'en remettent à Lui seul. Ce passage s'inscrit dans une exhortation adressée aux croyants faibles de La Mecque à émigrer vers la terre d'Allah, qui est vaste, et à ne pas laisser la crainte de la mort les en empêcher, car la mort atteint toute âme. La plupart des exégètes, comme al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, az-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi et Abu Hayyan, s'accordent sur le fait que la patience et la confiance en Dieu réunissent tout le bien, et que la récompense évoquée est celle des chambres du Paradis. Les divergences portent d'abord sur la lecture : Hamza et al-Kisa'i lisent « linathwiyannahum », c'est-à-dire « nous les installerons », tandis que les autres lisent « lanubawwi'annahum », « nous les ferons demeurer » ; al-Tabari juge que les deux sens sont proches. Elles portent aussi sur l'expression « ma terre est vaste » : Ibn Jubayr et Ata' y voient l'appel à quitter une terre de désobéissance, Mujahid l'appel au combat contre les ennemis d'Allah, Mutarrif une allusion à la miséricorde ou à la subsistance divines, et Abu al-'Aliya l'invitation à chercher les alliés d'Allah. Concernant le verset suivant, « combien de bêtes ne portent pas leur subsistance », al-Hasan et Mujahid entendent qu'elles ne thésaurisent pas, tandis qu'Ibn 'Abbas limite la thésaurisation à l'homme, à la fourmi et à la souris. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi et al-Shawkani rejettent comme faible le récit d'occasion de révélation lié à la faim, et al-Qurtubi souligne que le Prophète lui-même mettait de côté la provision annuelle de sa famille.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset vient après l'ordre donné aux croyants de quitter La Mecque, alors qu'ils craignaient la pauvreté et la faim dans une terre où ils n'avaient ni biens ni proches. Dieu affirme que de nombreuses créatures ne portent pas leur subsistance et n'en font pas de réserve pour le lendemain, et pourtant Dieu les nourrit ; il nourrira de même les croyants, car il entend leurs paroles et connaît ce que recèlent leurs cœurs. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Jawzi retiennent que le sens visé est que Dieu se charge de la subsistance de toutes ses créatures, en quelque lieu qu'elles soient. Presque tous s'accordent à dire que la « dabba » désigne tout être qui rampe ou marche sur la terre, et que « ne pas porter sa subsistance » signifie ne pas faire de réserves ni de gains. Ibn 'Abbas et Sufyan rapportent que seuls l'homme, la fourmi et la souris thésaurisent, ce que répètent al-Zamakhshari et d'autres. Quant à l'expression « ne porte pas », certains l'attribuent à la faiblesse de l'animal, d'autres à l'absence d'épargne, d'autres encore à l'idée que Dieu seul garantit la subsistance. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi et Ibn Kathir rattachent le verset à l'émigration et jugent l'épargne contraire à la certitude de la foi ; Ibn Kathir et al-Shawkani rapportent un hadith d'Ibn 'Umar sur le sujet mais le tiennent pour faible, car il contredit la conduite prouvée du Prophète qui mettait de côté la provision annuelle de sa famille. Al-Baydawi et Abu al-Su'ud y voient une comparaison : l'animal faible et l'homme fort reçoivent pareillement leur subsistance de Dieu, qui seul en est la cause.

Dieu dit à Son Prophète ﷺ que, s'il interrogeait les associateurs sur Celui qui a créé les cieux et la terre et assujetti le soleil et la lune, ils répondraient nécessairement : « Allah ». Dieu s'étonne alors de leur détournement de l'unicité divine alors qu'ils reconnaissent Sa seigneurie. Selon plusieurs commentateurs, ce verset s'inscrit dans un contexte de réconfort des croyants qui craignaient la pauvreté lors de l'émigration : Celui qui a créé les cieux et la terre est Celui qui nourrit les bêtes faibles qui ne thésaurisent pas leur subsistance, il n'y a donc pas lieu de craindre pour leur existence. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi et Ibn 'Ashur s'accordent à dire que le verset établit que les associateurs reconnaissent l'unicité de la seigneurie, et que leur refus de l'unicité dans l'adoration est étonnant. Al-Razi et al-Qurtubi expliquent que reconnaître la seigneurie implique de reconnaître la divinité, tandis qu'al-Alusi et Abu al-Su'ud considèrent que l'interrogation de « fa-anna yu'fakun » exprime le blâme et l'étonnement. Les commentateurs divergent sur le pronom de « lahu » dans « wa yaqdiru lahu » : al-Tabari et al-Baghawi le rapportent à la même personne, tandis qu'Abu Hayyan admet qu'il peut renvoyer à d'autres individus, certains recevant l'abondance et d'autres la gêne. La plupart insistent sur le fait que richesse et pauvreté sont une épreuve et une sagesse divines, et ne signifient pas à elles seules l'agrément ou la colère de Dieu, comme le notent al-Jaza'iri et Ibn 'Ashur. Ibn Sa'di tire de ce verset une argumentation étendue contre le culte des idoles.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset affirme que Dieu seul élargit la subsistance à qui Il veut parmi Ses serviteurs et la restreint à qui Il veut, selon Sa science de ce qui convient à chacun, et que tout cela procède de Sa sagesse et de Sa science qui embrasse toute chose. La plupart des exégètes, parmi lesquels al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi et al-Baydawi, s'accordent à voir dans l'aisance comme dans la gêne une épreuve : la richesse n'indique pas en soi l'agrément de Dieu, ni la pauvreté Sa colère, mais l'un et l'autre éprouvent si le serviteur remercie ou ingrate, s'il patiente ou s'emporte. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn 'Atiyya rattachent la parole à l'appel des croyants à émigrer, certains craignant la misère, et rappellent que Dieu pourvoit même aux bêtes. Al-Razi et al-Zamakhshari relèvent que la mention de la science ouvre des finesses sur la plénitude de la volonté et de la sagesse divines, et que le pronom « Lui » peut renvoyer à une même personne tantôt élargie tantôt restreinte, ou à une autre personne ; Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi et Ibn 'Ashur exposent ces deux lectures. Ibn Sa'di et al-Jaza'iri soulignent que le verset affirme à la fois l'unicité de la seigneurie et celle de l'adoration, et qu'il dénonce la contradiction des polythéistes qui reconnaissent Dieu comme créateur et pourvoyeur tout en Lui associant d'autres divinités. Tous s'accordent sur le fait que Dieu est savant de toute chose, rien de Ses serviteurs ni de leurs intérêts ne Lui échappant.

Les commentateurs expliquent que Dieu ordonne à Son Prophète ﷺ de demander aux associateurs qui a fait descendre l'eau du ciel pour faire revivre la terre après sa mort. Ils répondront tous que c'est Dieu, puis le Prophète doit louer Dieu pour la preuve ainsi établie contre eux, et la plupart d'entre eux ne raisonnent pas, c'est-à-dire ne voient pas la contradiction entre reconnaître la seigneurie de Dieu et Lui associer d'autres dieux. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi et Ibn 'Ashur s'accordent sur le fait que les païens de la Mecque reconnaissaient que Dieu est le Créateur, le Pourvoyeur et Celui qui fait revivre, et que le refus de l'association découle de cet aveu. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi comprennent le mot « louange » comme une action de grâce pour l'établissement de la preuve, ou pour la préservation du Prophète de pareille égarement, tandis qu'al-Razi relève qu'elle peut être une incise dans le discours, ou qu'elle met en évidence la contradiction de leurs propos. Al-Biqa'i et Ibn Sa'di estiment que la preuve oblige à reconnaître l'unicité de la divinité après celle de la seigneurie. Ibn 'Ashur précise que la louange vise l'ensemble des preuves précédentes et non le seul argument de la pluie, et que « la plupart » désigne ceux qui ont cru et ceux qui se sont obstinés.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset rabaisse la vie d'ici-bas, qu'il décrit comme un simple divertissement et un jeu, c'est-à-dire une jouissance qui distrait un moment puis disparaît, à la manière des enfants qui jouent un instant avant de se séparer. La vie de l'au-delà, en revanche, est la vie véritable et durable, sans mort. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Mujahid et Ibn 'Abbas expliquent que le mot al-hayawan désigne la vie permanente qui ne connaît ni fin ni mort. Abu 'Ubayda, al-Zajjaj et Ibn Qutayba estiment que hayawan et hayat ont le même sens, position que retiennent Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et al-Nasafi. Al-Zamakhshari, suivi d'al-Baydawi et d'Abu al-Su'ud, soutient que la forme fa'alan ajoute une idée de mouvement et de vitalité, ce qui renforce la notion de vie accomplie dans l'au-delà. Al-Razi distingue le jeu, qui désigne l'attention portée au faux, et le divertissement, qui désigne l'éloignement de la vérité. Ibn 'Ashur note que le verset s'adresse à la fois aux sages et au commun des gens. Ibn 'Uthaymin précise que les œuvres pieuses accomplies ici-bas relèvent de l'au-delà, car leur fruit s'y manifeste, et qu'elles ne sont donc pas du jeu. Les commentateurs s'accordent pour voir dans la réponse de « si » une proposition sous-entendue : si les gens savaient, ils ne préféreraient pas le périssable au durable. Le contexte est celui de la condamnation de l'association et de l'aveuglement des polythéistes face à l'au-delà.

Ce verset décrit des gens qui, montés sur un navire et saisis par la peur de la noyade, invoquent Dieu seul avec une foi sincère, puis, une fois sauvés et arrivés à terre, retournent à l'associationnisme. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur ce point : dans la détresse, ces hommes reconnaissent que seul Dieu peut les sauver, et c'est ce qui rend leur retour au polythéisme condamnable. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi insistent sur ce contraste entre la sincérité du danger et l'oubli qui suit la délivrance. Al-Baghawi rapporte, comme Ikrima, que les Arabes de l'époque préislamique jetaient leurs idoles à la mer lorsque la tempête s'élevait, en criant « ô Seigneur, ô Seigneur ». Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi et al-Nasafi voient dans l'expression « dévots sincères » une forme d'ironie, puisque ces hommes ne sont sincères que dans l'épreuve. Concernant la particule « liyakfurû », la plupart la lisent comme une lâm de finalité, c'est-à-dire que leur retour au shirk aboutit à renier le bienfait du salut et à jouir de la vie présente, tandis qu'Al-Zamakhshari, Al-Baghawi, Ibn Ajiba et Ibn Atiyya la comprennent comme une lâm d'injonction, sur le mode de la menace, ce que confirme la lecture avec sukun. Le Razi relève que la passion du monde empêche l'homme de revenir à la nature monothéiste qui est la sienne, et que, dans la détresse, celle-ci se réveille. Ibn Ashur rappelle enfin que les Arabes voyageaient surtout par terre et craignaient donc moins la mer.

Ce passage de la sourate al-Ankabut décrit des idolâtres qui, pris de peur sur un navire, invoquent Allah seul avec sincérité, puis, une fois sauvés et revenus sur la terre ferme, retournent à l'associationnisme. Les commentateurs expliquent que « pour qu'ils renient ce que Nous leur avons donné » signifie qu'ils nient le bienfait du salut. Quant à « et pour qu'ils jouissent », la lecture avec kasra (lam de finalité) et celle avec sukun (lam d'impératif de menace) sont discutées. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir et Ibn al-Jawzi donnent la préférence à la lecture avec sukun, qui exprime la menace et le blâme, tandis que al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan et Ibn Ashur admettent les deux lectures, en parlant parfois de lam de conséquence. Al-Razi et al-Qurtubi présentent les deux interprétations. Tous s'accordent sur la menace finale « ils sauront bientôt », et sur la contradiction entre la sincérité dans le danger et l'associationnisme dans l'aisance. La suite évoque le sanctuaire sacré sûr qui préserve les Quraych alors que les autres Arabes sont pillés. Al-Tabari et Qatada y voient une grâce qui exige la reconnaissance, et le faux auquel ils croient est l'associationnisme. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di et Ibn Ashur rappellent que la vie présente n'est que jeu et divertissement face à la vie durable de l'au-delà. Le passage se conclut par la promesse de guidance donnée à ceux qui combattent pour Allah, qu'al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi interprètent de façons variées, les uns comme le combat intérieur, les autres comme le combat extérieur.

Ce verset rappelle aux Quraychites une contradiction : lorsqu'ils embarquent et craignent la noyade, ils invoquent Dieu seul avec un culte sincère, mais dès qu'il les ramène sur la terre ferme, ils retombent dans l'associationnisme. Les commentateurs expliquent la formule « afin qu'ils renient ce que Nous leur avons donné » comme signifiant que ce retour à l'idolâtrie revient à renier le bienfait du salut. La lecture de « wa-liyatamatta'u » avec une lam vocalisée e sous-entend un ordre de menace, alors que la lecture avec une lam sukūn marque une finalité ou une conséquence ; al-Tabari retient la première, la jugeant plus cohérente avec le contexte de menace, et d'autres commentateurs la suivent. Le verset suivant rappelle le bienfait du sanctuaire sûr : les Arabes autour de La Mecque se razziaient mutuellement, tandis que ses habitants vivaient en paix, ce qui devait les conduire à la gratitude. Les avis divergent sur le sens de « le faux » : pour Qatada c'est l'associationnisme, pour Yahya ibn Salam c'est Iblis, pour d'autres ce sont les idoles. De même pour « le bienfait de Dieu » : Ibn Abbas y voit la santé, d'autres l'islam et la révélation, d'autres encore la nourriture et la sécurité accordées. Al-Razi et al-Zamakhshari soulignent qu'un bienfait aussi manifeste ne peut être accordé que par Dieu, ce qui rend son déni plus grave. Enfin, « ceux qui combattent pour Nous » désigne pour la plupart des exégètes le combat contre les ennemis de la foi, mais certains y incluent la lutte contre son propre âme et ses passions, ou l'action conforme à la science acquise ; ce sens large est mentionné par Ibn Kathir et d'autres comme l'orientation générale du verset.

Le sens apparent du verset est qu'il n'existe personne de plus injuste que celui qui forge un mensonge contre Dieu, en Lui attribuant un associé ou un fils, ou en Lui imputant l'ordre de commettre une turpitude, ou qui traite de mensonge la vérité après qu'elle lui est parvenue, c'est-à-dire le monothéisme, le Coran ou le Prophète ﷺ, et que la demeure de ces infidèles est la Géhenne. Les commentateurs expliquent que l'interrogation « n'est-ce pas » est une affirmation et non une véritable question, comme le montre le célèbre vers de Jarir qu'ils citent souvent. La plupart s'accordent sur le sens du faux témoignage, qui consiste à attribuer un associé à Dieu, et du démenti, qui consiste à rejeter la vérité. Ils divergent toutefois sur ce que désigne « la vérité » : al-Sudi et Ibn Shajara parlent du monothéisme, Yahya ibn Sallam du Coran, Ibn Shajara encore du Prophète ﷺ, et al-Qurtubi estime que chacune de ces lectures est incluse dans les autres. Al-Zamakhshari souligne que la formule « lorsqu'elle leur est parvenue » blâme la précipitation dans le rejet, sans examen. Pour le verset suivant, les commentateurs s'accordent sur le fait que ceux qui luttent pour Dieu seront guidés, mais ils diffèrent sur le sens du combat. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir y voient le combat contre les ennemis et la défense de la religion, al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas et Ibn al-Mubarak la lutte contre l'âme et ses passions, et Abu Sulayman al-Darani la mise en pratique de ce que l'on sait. Sur la guidance, al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Jawzi y voient l'affermissement et l'accroissement de la bonne direction, tandis qu'al-Sudi y voit le chemin du Paradis. Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi rappellent que Dieu est avec les bienfaisants, par son secours ici-bas et par la récompense dans l'au-delà.

Ce verset affirme que ceux qui combattent (jahadu) pour Dieu, c'est-à-dire qui font effort pour obtenir Son agrément, Dieu les guidera vers Ses voies, et qu'Il est avec les bienfaisants par Son soutien et Son aide. Les commentateurs s'accordent à donner au mot jihad un sens général. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Jawzi l'entendent d'abord comme le combat contre les ennemis de la foi, pour soutenir la religion de Dieu. Al-Hasan al-Basri, Abu Sulayman al-Darani, al-Qurtubi et Ibn al-Qayyim y incluent la lutte contre l'âme, les passions et le démon, qu'al-Hasan tient pour le plus grand jihad. Ibn Abbas le rapporte à l'obéissance à Dieu, et al-Zamakhshari élargit le sens à toute lutte contre l'âme, le démon et les ennemis de la religion. Sur le sens de la guidance, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi y voient la fermeté et la réussite dans le droit chemin, tandis que al-Suddi, al-Nasafi et Ibn Atiyya la rapportent à la voie menant au Paradis. Plusieurs savants, dont al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya et al-Qurtubi, rapportent que celui qui agit selon sa science reçoit une science qu'il ne connaissait pas. Al-Razi propose une lecture philosophique, selon laquelle la guidance découle de la réflexion sur les signes divins. Ibn Atiyya et al-Qurtubi notent que la révélation de ce verset précède l'obligation du combat armé. Quant à la présence divine, la plupart des commentateurs la comprennent comme aide et soutien, et Ibn al-Jawzi précise que ce sont les monothéistes ou les combattants.

The sura opens with the disjointed letters Alif Lam Mim, whose meaning most commentators leave to God; Ibn Abbas is reported to have said it means "I am God, the most knowing". The verse that follows, the commentators explain, means that God will not leave believers who say "we believe" without testing them, since trial is a constant law for His servants. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir read the opening question as a rebuke, and take the trial to mean hardship, harm and tests of faith. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi list its forms: leaving one's homeland, fighting enemies, enduring poverty and the loss of property and self. They add that God knows in advance who is sincere, but this knowledge must become visible to people so that judgment rests on deeds.

The commentators agree that the verses were revealed concerning groups of believers in Mecca or concerning particular events: some who complained of the idolaters' abuse, Ammar ibn Yasir who was tortured, Mihja, the freedman of Umar and the first Muslim martyr at Badr, or men who converted in Mecca and were overtaken while emigrating. Ibn Atiyya holds that the meaning remains valid for the community until the end of time, since trials persist on the frontiers of the Muslims, through captivity, illness and affliction, and al-Qurtubi endorses this view.

Opinions differ on the phrase "they will not be tested": Mujahid says it means "they will not be questioned", others say they will not be tried in their persons and property, and others that they will not be tested by commands and prohibitions. On whether the sura is Meccan or Medinan, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report several views, and most hold that it is Meccan.

In this verse God rebukes, through a rhetorical question, those who think people will be left alone simply because they say "We believe" without being tested. The point is that faith is not a mere word: God tests His servants with duties and trials so that the sincere can be distinguished from the liar. The commentators agree that the fitna here means a test, but they differ on its form. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean being tried in one's person and property, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi extend it to the hardships of religious duty, such as emigration, fighting, abandoning desires and patience under calamity. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that although the verse was revealed about a group in Mecca, such as 'Ammar ibn Yasir, its meaning remains valid in every age, since trial is a constant divine practice.

Several accounts of the occasion of revelation are given: Muslims in Mecca who complained of the polytheists' persecution, the death of Mihja, a freedman of 'Umar, at Badr, and the case of 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a. The commentators report these without firmly preferring one, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the scope of the verse exceeds any single case.

All agree that God knows in advance who is sincere and who is lying. Therefore "God will know" means that He will make this reality manifest in actual events, and that He will judge by what occurs. Al-Zamakhshari also mentions a reading attributed to 'Ali in which the verb is causative, meaning that God will make people know who is sincere and who is a liar.

This verse in al-Ankabut states that God does not leave believers to be content with saying "we believe" without being tested, and that this is His established practice with earlier peoples. The commentators explain that God knows people's hearts before the trial, and that the test aims to make the truthful and the liar appear in the visible world, so that reward and punishment follow what actually happens. They agree that fitna here means trial through hardship and obligations, such as suffering at the hands of opponents, giving up desires, emigration and fighting. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see in it consolation for believers, since prophets and their followers faced similar trials, and al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari cite on this the hadith of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt in al-Bukhari about the saw and the iron combs. Opinions differ on the occasion of revelation. Ibn Jurayj, reporting Ubayd Allah ibn Umayr, links the verse to Ammar ibn Yasir, who was tortured for his faith; al-Tabari also records the view that it concerns Meccan Muslims who were turned back when they tried to emigrate. Muqatil links it to Mihja', the freedman of Umar, who was killed at Badr. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that although revealed for a specific case, the verse remains valid for the whole community as long as trials continue on the frontiers. On the meaning of "fa-la-ya'lamanna", al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir understand it as "will make apparent and distinguish", while al-Razi, explaining divine knowledge, says God knows everything in advance but judgment falls on what has occurred. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari also report the reading of Ali ibn Abi Talib, "fa-yu'linanna", which may mean making known to people or marking with a sign.

The commentators read this verse as a rhetorical question rebuking those who do evil and imagine they can escape God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the "evil deeds" primarily to mean associating partners with God, while al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the occasion concerned Meccan opponents who persecuted believers, and that the wording is general and covers anyone who does wrong. The key word "outrun us" is explained by Mujahid and al-Tabari as "escape us" or "make us unable to punish them", and al-Zamakhshari adds that the wrongdoers do not really hope to escape, but act as though they could out of heedlessness and persistence in sin. The closing phrase "how evil is their judgment" is read as a condemnation of their assumption; grammarians such as al-Zajjaj, Ibn Kaysan and Abu Hayyan parse the word "what" in different ways, without altering the meaning. Al-Razi connects the verse to the preceding trial of believers: God's delay in punishing does not mean neglect, since His promise and threat are certain. Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi apply the warning to the unbeliever and, more broadly, to anyone who persists in sin.

This verse says that whoever hopes to meet God, meaning he hopes for His reward or fears resurrection and judgment, should know that the term God has set for resurrection and recompense will certainly come, and should prepare for it through good deeds; God hears what people say and knows their intentions. The commentators allow two senses of the word hope: hope for reward, as Sa'id ibn Jubayr and most exegetes take it, or fear of resurrection and reckoning, as Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Baghawi report; al-Zajjaj and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer hope. As for the meeting with God, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read it as a figure for arriving at the final outcome, through death, resurrection and reckoning, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy understand it as the reward itself. Al-Razi considers the reading as a vision of God linguistically weak, though Abu al-Su'ud notes it. Most understand the term ajal as death or the Day of Resurrection, and al-Qurtubi says the exegetes agree that the meaning is that whoever fears death should act righteously. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Juzayy take the verse as comfort for those who long to meet God. It fits the surrounding theme of trial and striving: al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir state that the benefit of striving returns to the one who strives, that God needs nothing from the worlds, and that those who believe and do good will have their misdeeds covered and receive a better reward. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi relate the occasion of revelation to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his mother, and Ibn Kathir mentions reports of believers tried in Mecca; the meaning remains general for anyone tested in faith.

This verse says that whoever strives in struggle gains only for himself, since the reward of the effort returns to him, and that God is self-sufficient and needs neither the obedience nor the effort of His creatures. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that striving here means patience in effort, whether in fighting the enemies, especially the polytheists, or in restraining one's own soul to obey God, and that the reward goes to the believer. Al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy hold that the word may mean fighting or struggle against oneself, and that the meaning stays the same in either case. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the context may refer to patience under the hardships suffered by Muslims before emigration, or to fighting in defence of Islam, and that both readings are possible. Al-Razi observes that the verse combines good news and warning, since God is absolutely rich and depends on no one. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi stress that God commanded and forbade out of mercy toward His servants, not out of need. Al-Razi also notes that the verse does not by itself prove that reward is owed to the deed, only that it is promised. The commentators therefore agree that the benefit returns to the person and that God is free of need, and they differ mainly over the precise sense of striving meant.

This verse in Surah al-Ankabut promises that those who believe and do righteous deeds will have their bad deeds covered and be rewarded with the best of what they did. The commentators agree that expiation means removing the sin, either by good deeds that outweigh it or by forgiveness, and that the best reward refers to the finest of their actions. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the believer who endures the persecution of the polytheists receives his full reward, and Ibn Kathir adds that God accepts a small good deed and multiplies it up to seven hundred times. Al-Razi notes two readings: the reward is given according to the best of their deeds, or it is greater than their deeds, as in the verse about ten times the good deed. He also says the reward may exceed Paradise, perhaps being the vision of God. Al-Zamakhshari distinguishes between Muslims whose minor sins are overwhelmed by their good deeds and polytheists who convert and whose Islam erases what came before. Ahmad, responding to him, criticises his view that a grave sin without repentance is punished. Al-Razi holds that faith and works are distinct yet linked, and that good works must be done sincerely for God's sake to be accepted. Ibn Ashur sees this verse as a promise following the earlier threat. Ibn Sa'di stresses that good deeds erase bad ones and that obedience is the best of works. The scholars differ mainly on how expiation works, on the meaning of the best reward, and on the status of grave sins, though none doubts the general promise.

This verse commands people to be good to their parents, but if the parents strive to make them associate with God what they have no knowledge of, they must not obey them, since all return to God, who will inform them of what they did. The commentators agree that obedience to parents never extends to disobeying the Creator, and that the duty of kindness toward them remains even if they are disbelievers. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the verse was revealed about Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, whose mother swore she would neither eat nor drink until he abandoned Islam; the Prophet told him to treat her kindly without obeying her in polytheism. Ibn 'Atiyya and others mention a second report that it concerned 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, while Ibn 'Abbas and others hold that its ruling is general. On the grammar of the word 'hasanan', the Basran grammarians take it as an object of an implied repetition of the verb, whereas the Kufans take it as an implied verb meaning to do good. Al-Razi notes that the indefinite form signals perfection. As for the reward of believers who do righteous deeds, the commentators understand it as their admission among the righteous, that is, into Paradise.

The commentators explain that this verse promises those who believe in God and His Messenger and do righteous deeds that they will be counted among the righteous. Al-Baghawi says this means the prophets and the saints, while al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya take it to mean the place of the righteous, namely Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud combine both readings: the highest degree of righteousness is the goal the prophets wished for, and it leads to Paradise. Al-Tabari specifies that righteous deeds mean performing God's obligations and avoiding what He forbids.

The verse follows the instruction to be kind to one's parents, which must not extend to obeying them in associating partners with God. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the promise of being counted among the righteous consoles the believer who suffers estrangement from his family. Al-Razi observes that the verse repeats the situation of the guided believer, set against that of the misguided.

Opinions differ on the passage that follows. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi apply it to hypocrites or to believers forced to leave Mecca, while others link it to Ammar ibn Yasir or Mihja'. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur stress the general scope of the text beyond the particular case. All agree that being among the righteous is a high reward.

This verse describes people who profess faith only with their tongues: when they suffer harm for God's sake, they treat men's persecution as if it were God's punishment, turn away and abandon their faith; yet when victory comes from their Lord, they claim they were with the believers all along. God replies that He knows best what is in the hearts. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi understand the speakers as hypocrites who apostatise under trial, a reading also held by al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, while al-Qurtubi notes that the hypocrites are the main target. On the occasion of revelation, Ibn Abbas reports that it concerns Meccan believers forced out with the idolaters towards Badr, Mujahid speaks of believers who yield to hardships, al-Dahhak of Meccan hypocrites who revert to polytheism, and Qatada of those sent back to Mecca by the polytheists. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir also mention 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a, and Mawardi and al-Razi distinguish the one forced to deny outwardly while his heart remains firm in faith. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi observe that the trial turns people away from faith just as God's punishment turns people away from disbelief. Al-Razi, Ibn Ashur and Ibn Sa'di emphasise that this trial is a divine test that separates the sincere from the liar. Most commentators therefore see in the verse a warning against wavering under trial and a promise to the patient believers.

This verse states that God will make manifest the true state of the believers and of the hypocrites, distinguishing the sincere from the false through trial and testing. The commentators agree on this meaning: the distinction is made through hardships and tribulations, and the divine knowledge mentioned refers to the public manifestation of each person's condition and the recompense that follows, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that the testing comes through adversity as well as ease, and that the steadfast believer holds firm in trouble while the hypocrite turns back at the first harm. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the hypocrites believed God would not know what was in their hearts, which is why the verse stresses the point with an oath and emphatic forms; Ibn 'Ashur adds that the aim is retribution according to what God knows of each person. Opinions differ on who is meant. According to Mujahid, they are people who profess faith with their tongues and waver in misfortune; according to Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima, they are believers whom the pagans forced out to Badr and who then apostatised; according to Qatada, they are those the polytheists sent back to Mecca; one report also names 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'a. Al-Baghawi and al-Tabari nonetheless give the general sense, applying to anyone tested for the sake of his faith. The commentators do not choose among these views, and the common meaning remains the same: the trial separates the steadfast believer from the fickle hypocrite.

This verse reports the words of the disbelievers of Quraysh to those among them who had believed: follow our path, and we shall bear your sins, should there be a resurrection and a reckoning. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, whom al-Qurtubi follows, explain that the imperative form carries the sense of a condition: if you follow our path, we shall bear your sins. Al-Zamakhshari adds that they commanded themselves to bear the burden so that both demands would be fulfilled together, and some commentators name al-Walid ibn al-Mughira as the speaker. All agree on God's rebuttal: they will not bear the sins of others in any way, since no one carries another's burden. Regarding the next verse, most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya, take the burdens to be their own sins together with the sins of those they misled, citing the hadith that whoever calls to misguidance bears the sins of those who follow him without their own burden being reduced. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that others understood these burdens as the sins of supporters of tyrants, of innovators, or of those who establish unjust customs, and he holds that the hadith encompasses all these meanings. On the word 'liars', al-Zamakhshari offers two readings: one who guarantees what he cannot fulfil is not strictly a liar by definition, yet they are liars either because their pledge contradicts reality or because their hearts disagree with their words. The occasion of revelation is also reported differently across the accounts.

This verse reports that the disbelievers told those who had believed among them: follow our path, and we will bear your sins, if there is indeed a resurrection and reckoning. God refutes them: they will not carry anything of the sins of others. He then states that they will carry their own burdens and, in addition, further burdens, those of the people they misled, without any reduction in the burdens of those who followed them, and that on the Day of Resurrection they will be questioned in rebuke about what they used to fabricate. The commentators agree that the verse refutes the disbelievers' claim and affirms that no one bears another's sin. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and the Jalalayn hold that the one who calls to misguidance carries his own burden and the burden of those who followed him, supported by the well-known hadith that whoever calls to misguidance bears a burden like that of those who follow him. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand the extra burdens as the load of misleading others and of having caused their error. Al-Mawardi offers three readings: the helpers of oppressors, the innovators in religion, and those who establish unjust customs. Ibn 'Atiyya considers that the hadith gathers all these meanings. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur read this burden as an image of increased punishment rather than a transfer of responsibility. On the word nahmil, Mujahid explains it as guaranteeing rather than physically carrying. Regarding the occasion of revelation, Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti report that the statement came from the leaders of Quraysh, possibly al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, addressed to weak believers. All agree on the principle that each soul bears the consequences of its own deeds.

This verse tells that Allah sent Noah to his people, and that he stayed among them for a thousand years minus fifty, calling them to monotheism and to abandoning idols, until the flood seized them while they were wronging themselves through their polytheism. The commentators agree that the story serves to console the Prophet Muhammad and to strengthen his patience in the face of his people's harm. They also note that the exception in the number confirms the precision of the figure and removes any sense of approximation. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the word tufan originally means anything that overwhelms something in abundance, but here it refers to water. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada take it to mean rain, al-Dahhak takes it as drowning, and a report from 'A'isha takes it as death. On Noah's lifespan the views differ widely: Ibn 'Abbas says he was sent at forty and lived sixty years after the flood, while Ka'b al-Ahbar, 'Awn ibn Abi Shaddad and Qatada give other figures, and the commentators do not choose among them. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari offer another reason for the wording, namely magnification and exact precision. As for the ship, which the verse calls a sign for all peoples, Ibn Kathir reads it as the vessel itself or as the type of ships, al-Tabari allows that the pronoun may refer to the punishment, and Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan record the same possibility.

This verse says that God saved Noah and those who were in the ark with him, and made the ark, or the whole event, a sign for people. The commentators agree that the saved were Noah, his family and the believers with him, and that the pronoun in 'made it a sign' most often refers to the ark. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, following Qatada, that the ark remained visible on al-Judi, while Ibn Kathir adds that the word may mean its kind rather than the very vessel. Ibn 'Ashur confirms that remains were seen for a long time. Al-Razi gives several reasons why it was a sign: it was built before the flood by revelation, God protected it from violent winds, and it provided provisions. He also allows that the pronoun may refer to the event or to the deliverance. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud mention the same two options. Opinions differ on the number of those aboard: Ibn Abbas and others give eighty or seventy-eight, Ibn Ishaq ten. On the meaning of 'flood', Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada say rain, al-Dahhak says drowning, and others say death. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di read the passage as a consolation to the Prophet, showing that earlier prophets endured hardship before him.

This verse recounts Abraham's call to his people to worship God alone and to be mindful of Him, saying that this is better for them if they have knowledge. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain it as devoting worship to God alone, performing His obligations and avoiding what He forbids. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud stress above all not associating anything with God, while the two Jalals understand taqwa as fear of His punishment. The commentators agree that the idols are statues that can neither benefit nor harm. On the phrase 'wa takhluquna ifkan', Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari take it to mean fashioning or carving, whereas Mujahid, Qatada and al-Hasan take it to mean inventing falsehood; al-Tabari prefers the standard reading. Most scholars hold that the idols cannot provide any sustenance, so God directs people to seek their provision from Him alone, to worship Him and to give thanks. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi link the following lines to a consolation for the Prophet, noting that earlier nations also denied their messengers and that the messenger's duty is only clear transmission, while Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi see these as Abraham's own words. Grammarians discuss the parsing of 'Ibrahim' and 'idh' and the readings in the nominative or accusative. All commentators note the closing reference to the return to God and to resurrection.

This part of verse 17 of Surah al-Ankabut calls people to worship God alone. The commentators place it in the story of Abraham, who called his people to worship God and fear Him. They agree that the idols they worshipped were only made objects. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explain that the phrase 'and you fabricate a lie' means that you carve these idols with your hands and call them gods, or that you lie in calling them gods and intercessors with God. Al-Tabari holds that the verb means to make or carve, while others, as reported by Ibn Kathir, understand it as to lie and invent. Variant readings noted by al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan add nuances without changing the general sense. The verse then argues from an observable fact: these idols cannot provide any sustenance. God therefore commands people to seek sustenance from Him alone, to worship Him and to give thanks. Al-Razi explains that the indefinite noun in the negative clause means they can grant nothing at all, while the definite noun in the positive clause means all provision is with God, a view also held by Ibn Juzayy and al-Zamakhshari. The passage ends by reminding people that they will return to God after death, as Ibn Sa'di, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi develop. Commentators differ on who speaks the sentence 'if you deny, nations before you have denied': Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Shawkani attribute it to Abraham, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir allow that it may be an inserted divine statement. All agree that the aim is to break with idolatry and call to monotheism.

This part of the verse states that those who deny the Messenger are not the first to do so, since earlier peoples also cried lies, among them 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Lot according to al-Samani and al-Baghawi, and they were punished. It therefore contains a warning to the deniers. As for the Messenger's duty, it is only to convey the message clearly. Al-Tabari explains that the 'clear delivery' is one whose meaning the hearer understands and grasps. Al-Razi says that conveying means presenting the matters, while clarifying means establishing proof, and he concludes that delaying the explanation beyond the time of need is not permitted. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud consider that the verse may be part of Abraham's speech to his people, whereas Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Tabari take it as God's address to the Quraysh. Ibn Juzayy also allows that it may be a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ, drawing on the example of earlier prophets. The readings differ on the verb 'see' and on the word nash'a, which Abu Hayyan discusses at length. Commentators generally agree that the verse is both a threat and a consolation, and that the responsibility for rejection rests with the one who rejects.

This verse states that God originates creation and then brings it back, and that restoring it is as easy for Him as originating it. The commentators read the opening question as a rebuke addressed to those who deny resurrection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the seeing refers to the development of man from a drop, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, and that the return is resurrection after death. Ibn Jarir and Qatada prefer to see it as a seeing of the mind through reasoning. Al-Zamakhshari holds that "then He brings it back" is not coordinated with "He originates", but is a separate statement about resurrection; Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy follow this reading. Ibn Juzayy also mentions that the return may mean the yearly renewal of plants, though he judges the first reading more fitting. Al-Razi notes that the first creation from dust is harder to grasp than rebuilding from material already prepared.

The commentators agree on the core meaning: resurrection is possible and easy for God, and it can be inferred from observing creation. They differ on the grammar, on the sense of "seeing", and on how the two acts are compared. Ibn Ashur explains that the two verbs are used together as a pair meaning to originate and restore, and that the question is meant to draw attention. Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan and Ibn al-Jawzi, also note the variant readings of the verbs and of the word for creation.

God instructs His Prophet to tell those who deny the resurrection to travel through the earth and observe how creation began, so that from what they see they may infer that God can bring creation back after it perishes. The commentators explain that "the final creation" means the resurrection after death. The words "God is capable of all things" mean that He can accomplish both the first creation and the second. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy agree that this is evidence for the resurrection: whoever began creation is not too weak to repeat it. Ibn Juzayy notes that "then He repeats it" is a separate statement rather than something seen. Ibn Ashur explains that travelling exposes a person to many kinds of creatures and to the remains of past peoples, prompting reflection on how things came into being from nothing. Al-Razi observes that the divine name is made explicit in the second clause to strengthen the affirmation of the resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud report that some take the passage as Abraham's words to his people, while others read it as addressed directly to the Quraysh. Readers differ on the word "nash'a", pronounced with or without a long vowel, but all treat the two forms as having the same meaning. Ibn Uthaymin adds that travel may be physical, mental, or both, with reflection being essential.

This verse states that God punishes whom He wills and shows mercy to whom He wills, and that all return is to Him alone. Al-Tabari explains that this refers to the resurrection after death: God punishes those who committed sins during their lives and shows mercy to those who repent, believe and do good. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di present it as God's absolute authority, which no one can question, and as perfect justice. The commentators agree that the divine will applies to those who deserve punishment or mercy, and that these decisions follow wisdom, so no one is punished without deserving it. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that punishment is mentioned first because the address is to those who deny the resurrection, with mercy following as a source of hope. Al-Mawardi, transmitted by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Sam'ani, suggests that punishment and mercy may also take place in this world, such as punishment through greed or bad character and mercy through contentment or good character; the other commentators do not settle this reading. The verse then affirms that human beings cannot escape God either on earth or in the sky, and have no protector or helper besides Him. Scholars differ on the meaning of 'nor in the sky': al-Farra' and Ibn Zayd read it as 'nor whoever is in the sky', Qutrub as 'even if you were in it', while others take it as referring to heights and fortresses. All agree, however, that the verse asserts God's comprehensive power and human powerlessness.

The commentators explain that this verse states that people cannot escape God's power, neither on earth nor in heaven, and that apart from Him they have neither a protector who guards them nor a helper who saves them. They differ on the meaning of the mention of heaven. Al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd and al-Farra' read it as saying that the inhabitants of earth cannot overpower God on earth, nor the inhabitants of heaven in heaven should they disobey Him, in the manner of Hassan ibn Thabit's verse; Qutrub takes it to mean that even if you were in heaven you would not overpower Him. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan keep the literal sense of height, saying that neither fortified towers nor lofty places offer refuge. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi connect the verse to the proof of resurrection from the initial creation and from reflection on the cosmos, and recall that God punishes whom He wills and shows mercy to whom He wills, and that to Him all return. The exegetes define the wali as the close one who manages affairs and the nasir as the one who repels harm; al-Razi shows that flight and resistance are both impossible. Al-Mawardi offers several readings of divine will tied to human conduct. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Sa'di stress that punishment and mercy follow deeds, and that the disbelievers despair of God's mercy.

This verse states that those who disbelieved in Allah's signs, meaning His proofs in creation and the Qur'an, and denied the meeting with Him, meaning resurrection and judgment, have despaired of His mercy and will suffer a painful punishment. The commentators agree that this despair will occur on the Day of Resurrection and that the verse is a warning, though some note that the disbeliever has no hope of mercy in this life, so the statement also describes their state. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi explain that mercy here means Paradise, while Ibn Jurayj and others understand it as forgiveness. Al-Tabari adds that this will happen in the afterlife when they see the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari reads the past tense as expressing a certain outcome, and al-Razi observes that mercy is attributed to God while punishment is not, which indicates that mercy precedes wrath.

Some scholars treat the verse as a parenthetical address to the Meccans inserted within Abraham's story, the preceding verses serving as reminder and warning, while others take it as Abraham's own words. Readings of the word yaʾisu also differ. Al-Farra' and Ibn Zayd explain that the sense parallels the phrase 'nor whoever is in the heavens', meaning that no one can frustrate God.

The commentators agree that faith in God's mercy is accompanied by hope and fear, whereas the disbeliever feels neither, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note. Ibn Juzayy suggests the verse may describe the disbeliever's state in this world, while others see it as a statement of their despair on the Day of Judgment. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Razi identify rejection of the Qur'an and of resurrection as the cause of this despair, and the repeated demonstrative underlines that they deserve it.

This verse describes the reaction of Abraham's people, who, unable to answer his arguments, said only: kill him or burn him. The commentators debate who spoke these words. Al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that one of them may have said it while the others consented; al-Razi says the notables spoke and their followers carried out the order. All report that they threw him into the fire and that God saved him. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn say God made the fire cool and safe for him. Ka'b al-Ahbar and al-Tabari say only his bonds were burned, and al-Zamakhshari reports that the fire harmed nothing that day.

The commentators agree that this deliverance is a sign. Al-Razi explains the plural "signs" by the wondrous nature of the rescue, compared with Noah's ark, which was a single sign; Ibn 'Ashur holds that it is a sign for every witness. Several, including Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn Sa'di, stress that only believers benefit from such signs.

The rest of the passage is read by most as Abraham's rebuke of his people for taking idols out of mutual affection in this life, while on the Day of Resurrection they will disown and curse one another, with the Fire as their abode. Commentators differ on the grammar of the phrase "affection between you": al-Baghawi and Abu Hayyan record several readings and constructions without deciding between them. Ibn Kathir sees in it a reproach of their attachment to idolatry.

The Qur'an quotes Abraham's words to his people after God saved him from the fire: you have taken idols apart from God only as a bond of affection between you in the life of this world; then on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another and curse one another, and the Fire will be your abode, with no helpers for you. The readers differ on how to vocalise the word mawadda and its construction with baynakum. Some read it in the accusative, unnunated, with baynakum as a place adverb; others read it in the nominative, in construct. The commentators judge these readings close in meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that you took these idols so that you would love one another and unite in their worship, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya take the nominative as a predicate of an implied subject, meaning that what you took as idols is a source of affection among you. Al-Razi holds that the affection lies between the idols and their worshippers, since whoever is dominated by bodily pleasures does not turn to the pleasures of the intellect. Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi list the grammatical options without preferring one. All agree on the outcome: this worldly affection ends, leaders disown their followers and followers curse their leaders, and the same Fire awaits all of them. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim add that every friendship built on falsehood turns into enmity on that Day, while some exclude the God-fearing. Most commentators say nothing more on this verse, and they differ only slightly over who speaks the next words, 'I migrate to my Lord.'

The commentators explain that this verse describes Lot's belief in Abraham: he confirmed Abraham's message when Abraham called his people to worship God alone. For al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, the words "I am migrating to my Lord" are most likely spoken by Abraham himself, announcing that he is leaving the land of his idolatrous people to go wherever his Lord commands; al-Tabari identifies the destination as the Levant, and Qatada reports that the departure was from Kuthà, near Kufa, to Harran and then to the Levant. Ibn Jurayj and others say he first went to Harran before being ordered to the Levant. Ibn Kathir notes that the pronoun could also refer to Lot, but he prefers Abraham.

The commentators agree that migrating to God means leaving for a place where God can be worshipped and His religion practised. Al-Razi argues that such a departure becomes necessary once preaching can no longer guide the people, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya take the preposition to express the seeking of God's pleasure. Ibn Atiyya notes that in legal usage a "muhajir" is one who leaves his homeland out of desire for God's approval.

The closing words, "He is the Mighty, the Wise", are read by al-Tabari as meaning that God protects His servants from their enemies and manages His creation with wisdom; al-Razi and al-Baydawi take them as assurance that God commands only what is good.

On Lot's kinship, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir call him Abraham's nephew, while al-Zamakhshari describes him as the son of Abraham's sister. Ibn Ashur also reports that Lot was the only one of his people to believe in Abraham, in line with Ibn Ishaq.

This verse says that God gave Abraham Isaac, and after him Jacob as a grandson, placed prophethood and the Book among his descendants, granted him his reward in this world, and that he is among the righteous in the Hereafter. The commentators agree that most prophets after Abraham descended from him and that the revealed Books, the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and the Qur'an, came through his line. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that Ishmael is not named because his status was well known, while al-Alusi notes that the verse is a gift of descendants granted in old age. As for the reward in this world, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean a good reputation, and Qatada and Ibn Kathir add that the followers of every religion claim him and approve of him. Al-Suddi understands it as a righteous son, others as seeing his place in Paradise, and al-Mawardi as the continuation of his hospitality at his grave, which he holds to be unique to him. Al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari hold that this reward does not reduce his reward in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di link it to his patience in preaching and his migration to his Lord. On who said "I am migrating", al-Nakha'i and Qatada attribute it to Abraham, while another view ascribes it to Lot, though most hold it is Abraham.

The verse recalls Lot's rebuke to his people, who committed an abomination no one among the peoples had committed before them, namely the sodomy of men. Commentators agree that it was an extremely grave sin whose unprecedented nature is underlined by the fact that human nature recoils from it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya describe it as men having intercourse with men through the anus. As for 'cutting off the path', views differ: Ibn Zayd and al-Qurtubi understand highway robbery, the seizing and killing of travellers; al-Qurtubi also reports Ibn Shajara's view that they forced travellers into the act, while al-Hasan and al-Mawardi take it to mean cutting off offspring by turning from women to men. On the 'blameworthy acts in their gatherings', the reports vary: 'A'isha and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad mention flatulence, Umm Hani relates from the Prophet that they pelted passers-by with pebbles and mocked them, Mujahid says they had intercourse with one another openly, and Ibn 'Abbas lists a range of conduct. Al-Tabari prefers the report of Umm Hani, while Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi extend the term to any improper conduct. Their answer was a challenge: let the punishment of God come upon them. Lot then asked his Lord for help against these corrupters. Several scholars, including al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, draw from the verse support for a legal penalty for sodomy, comparable to that for fornication, while others leave the matter to natural revulsion as a deterrent.

The verse recounts Lot's rebuke to his people, whom he accuses of committing an abomination no one in the worlds had committed before them, namely intercourse with men, and of also cutting off the road and committing reprehensible acts in their gatherings. The commentators agree that the abomination is sodomy. On the meaning of cutting off the road, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya take it as highway robbery, killing, or harassing passers-by, while al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that they forced travellers into such acts so that people avoided the route; al-Mawardi, al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi also mention the cutting of progeny through turning away from women. For the reprehensible acts in their assembly, al-Tabari adopts, on the authority of Umm Hani's hadith from the Prophet, that they pelted passers-by with pebbles and mocked them, a view also cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Razi. Mujahid and Qatada understood it as men having relations with one another in their gatherings, 'A'isha and Ibn 'Abbas as breaking wind openly, and others mention pigeon-racing, whistling, or loosening garments. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim report these without deciding, while Zamakhshari and Qurtubi list them together as all having been practised. Their answer to the warning was a challenge: bring the punishment of God if you are truthful. Most commentators say Lot then asked his Lord for help against these corrupters.

This verse records Lot's prayer against his people after he had condemned their vile deed and their other abominations, and they had refused to repent and challenged him to bring God's punishment. He said: "My Lord, help me against the corrupting people." The commentators explain that the help he asks for is the sending of the punishment, and that calling them corrupters was meant to hasten it, since they had invented this vice and made it customary among those who came after them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi agree that their corruption lay in drawing people into sins and vile acts, and that God answered the prayer by sending the angels to destroy the town. The vile deed itself is taken by most to be intercourse with men. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others report varied accounts of the reprehensible acts in their gatherings: pelting passers-by with stones and mocking them, breaking wind, playing with pigeons, whistling, and undoing garment buttons. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi suggest that all of these were practised among them. On the phrase "cutting off the road", the commentators give three meanings: highway robbery with killing and plunder, stopping travellers to force them into the vice until people stopped passing, or cutting off offspring by turning away from women. Al-Razi explains that Lot asked for their destruction because their non-existence was better than their existence, since they corrupted both the present and the future. Ibn 'Ashur sees the help sought as the punishment of those who denied the message, so that its truth would become manifest. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that scholars differ on the penalty for sodomy, some requiring death, some the penalty for adultery, and others no legal penalty, and he reports these opinions without choosing between them.

This passage tells how messengers of God, the angels, came to Abraham with the good news of Isaac, and of Jacob after him, and then told him they were sent to destroy the people of the town, which the commentators identify as Sodom, the town of Lot's people. They gave as the reason that its people were wrongdoers, meaning they wronged themselves through disbelief and sin and wronged others. The commentators agree that the good news was the birth of a son and then of his son, and that the town is Sodom, and that wrongdoing includes disbelief and all kinds of sins. Some report, citing Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, the evils of Lot's people: they practised sodomy in their gatherings, broke wind openly, and pelted passers-by with pebbles. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also mention that they waylaid travellers. Opinions differ on the meaning of wrongdoing: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it as denying the truth and disobeying God, while al-Razi argues that the angels mention it only to justify the destruction and not as a description of the present. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the past tense shows the wrongdoing was persistent. All agree that Lot was in the town. Abraham points this out, and the angels reply that they know better who is there, that they will save Lot and his family except his wife, who will be among those left behind to perish. Readers differ between the lighter and the intensified form of the verb for saving, two forms with the same meaning.

This verse gives the continuation of the dialogue between Abraham and the angels, who had announced the destruction of Lot's town for the wrongdoing of its people. Abraham said that Lot was there; the angels replied that they knew best who was in it, that they would save Lot and his family except his wife, who would be among those left behind to face punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud agree that the angels reassured Abraham: Lot would be saved, and his wife would perish with the people, because she backed them in their disbelief. On the meaning of al-Ghabirin, opinions differ: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud read it as those who remain in the punishment or in ruin, while another view, cited by Ibn 'Atiyya, takes it as those who remain alive. Al-Alusi notes that the wording allows both senses. Al-Zamakhshari explains that Abraham's reply was a plea out of compassion for Lot and the believers rather than a claim that Lot was present. Al-Razi observes that the angels combined good news with warning. Ibn 'Atiyya reports from Ibn 'Abbas that Abraham sought to save the believers in the town. The commentators also agree on the role of Lot's wife, who assisted her people, and on the rain of stones that destroyed the town, whose traces remain a sign for those who reflect, though they differ on what those traces are: stones, black water or ruins.

This passage describes the moment the messengers, who are angels, arrive at Lot. He was distressed by their coming and his resources ran short, because he took them for men and feared for them from his people, who were known for their depravity. The angels reassure him that he should neither fear nor grieve, for he and his family will be saved except his wife, who was among those who would remain behind in punishment. The commentators agree that 'sāʾa bihim' means he was grieved out of fear for his guests, and that 'ḍāqa bihim dharʿan' is a figure for lacking the capacity to cope. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report that the angels appeared as handsome young men, which deepened his anxiety. The phrase 'al-ghabirin' is read in two ways: most, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, take it to mean those left behind in punishment, while others, as Ibn 'Atiyya reports, take it to mean those who lived on through long life. Al-Razi notes that Lot's wife pointed the people to the guests and so shared in their fate. The readings of 'linunajjiyannahu' and 'munajjūka' vary between doubled and single consonants, forms the exegetes regard as equivalent. As for the 'rijz' from heaven, some understand stones, others a sinking of the land or a shower of pebbles. All agree that the lasting sign, 'āyatan bayyinatan', is a trace of the town, but they differ on its nature: Ibn 'Abbas says the ruins of their dwellings, Qatada the stones, and Mujahid the black water on the surface of the earth.

This verse reports that the messengers told Lot they would send down upon the people of this town, Sodom, a punishment from heaven because of their defiance and their deviation from obedience to God, namely the grave sin they committed. The commentators agree that rijz means punishment. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and the authors of the Jalalayn describe it as a chastisement from the sky, while al-Baghawi, citing Muqatil, understands it as a sinking of the ground and a shower of stones. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the root refers to the agitation that seizes the one who is punished. As for the "clear sign" left from that town, opinions differ: Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it to be the ruins of their dwellings, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya take it to be the stones that fell upon them, and Mujahid takes it to be the black water covering the ground. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi observe that these views can be combined without contradiction.
