Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi, describe the reprehensible acts practised in their gatherings, such as pelting passers-by with pebbles and mocking strangers, citing transmitted reports. Al-Alusi and Ibn Sa'di note that this punishment came in response to Lot's prayer against his people.

The commentators explain that this verse speaks of a clear trace left behind by the town that God destroyed, Sodom, where Lot's people lived, after He sent down punishment on them for their wickedness. The meaning most of them agree on is that God preserved from those dwellings a plain sign and a clear lesson for people who reflect. They also agree that the verse calls for contemplation and taking heed, and that the reason meant here is the reason of discernment and right guidance, not mere perception.

They differ, however, on what this sign is. Ibn 'Abbas says it is the ruined traces of their dwellings, a view taken up by Zamakhshari, Abu al-Su'ud and Alusi. Qatada says it is the stones with which they were destroyed, some of which were said to have survived until the first generations of this community, while Mujahid says it is the black water that appears on the surface of the earth. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the remains now submerged under the waters of Lot's lake are part of this sign, and that the word "clear" shows it endures over time, unlike the sign of the ark.

Some exegetes, such as Baydawi and Nasafi, note that the verb "left" means "preserved", and that the phrase "for a people" attaches either to this verb or to the word "clear". Ibn Kathir adds that reflecting on these ruins should lead people to think about what they see and what they hear reported.

The commentators explain that God sent Shu'ayb to the people of Madyan, who were his kin, and he called them to worship God alone and to hope for reward on the Last Day, that is, to act in ways that merit a good recompense, and he forbade them to spread corruption on earth. The commentators agree that the plain meaning of the command to worship is monotheism, and that the corruption forbidden includes sins and wrongdoing. They also agree that denying the prophet brought on their destruction by the violent quake called al-rajfa, which some identify as a cry from Gabriel; Ibn Kathir and others say the cry caused the quake. Ibn Kathir lists among their wrongs cheating in measure and weight and highway robbery. Al-Tabari explains that corruption means persisting in and multiplying disobedience to God. The meaning of 'hope' divides the scholars: Abu 'Ubayda, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Sam'ani read it as fear, a view some grammarians dispute without a negation, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read it as doing the deeds that lead to reward, and al-Razi finds hope fitting because worshipping God brings good in both abodes. On the word 'abode', some take it to mean the town and others the houses. Madyan names both the tribe and the place. On the word 'discerning', Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it to mean they were blinded in their error and proud of it, al-Farra' takes it to mean people endowed with insight, and others say they thought they were rightly guided.

This verse tells that the people of Madyan denied their prophet Shu'ayb, and the quake seized them, so that by morning they lay dead in their homes. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: al-raj fa is a violent quake, and jathimin describes bodies lying prostrate and lifeless. Qatada explicitly says they were dead. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi take the quake itself as the cause of death. Others, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, report that the Cry of Gabriel made hearts tremble and shook the land; Abu Hayyan and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the cry caused the quake, so that the two accounts do not conflict.

Opinions also differ on the word dar. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain the singular as avoiding ambiguity, while others understand it as the town or the dwellings. Al-Razi notes that the singular here and the plural in other surahs reflect a nuance about the force of the punishment.

The commentators recall Shu'ayb's call: worship God, hope for the Last Day, and do not spread corruption on earth. They differ on the sense of hope. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi read it as fear of the Last Day, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read it as doing the deeds that lead to reward. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy identify the corruption as cheating in weights and measures and robbing travellers. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qasimi note that warning comes before punishment in the prophetic pattern.

All the commentaries agree that the story is a lesson for mankind, and that rejecting the messengers brings divine punishment.

This verse recalls the destruction of 'Ad and Thamud, the people of Hud and of Salih. The commentators explain that the ruins of their dwellings, which the Quraysh passed on their journeys, were clear evidence of what had befallen them. Satan made their deeds, namely idolatry and sins, seem fair to them and turned them away from the right path. On the phrase 'and they were clear-sighted', most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Muqatil and al-Kalbi, take it to mean that they were pleased with their misguidance and thought they were right. Al-Farra' understands it as people endowed with reason and insight whose insight did not profit them. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud explain that they had the capacity to reflect and to discern, or that they knew punishment was coming through the warnings of the messengers yet persisted stubbornly until they perished. Ibn Kathir places the verse within a list of nations that rejected their messengers. The commentators draw no legal rulings from this verse; they focus on describing the destruction, its cause, and the meaning of clear-sightedness.

This verse mentions Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman, to whom Moses brought clear signs, yet they grew arrogant on earth and could not escape God. The commentators explain that these men could not outrun God's power, and that He punished them after establishing proof against them. They agree that Qarun was swallowed by the earth, that Pharaoh and his people were drowned, and that arrogance was the cause of their ruin. Opinions differ on the peoples named in the following verse. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj assign the hasib (a storm of stones or wind carrying pebbles) to the people of Lot and the cry (al-sayha) to Thamud, while Qatada assigns the cry to the people of Madyan. Al-Tabari holds that the cry concerns both Thamud and Madyan, since God did not restrict it to one of them. On the drowning, Ibn 'Abbas attributes it to the people of Noah, Qatada to the people of Pharaoh, and al-Tabari holds that both are meant. Ibn 'Atiyya suggests that 'Ad may also be included under the hasib, since that wind hurled harmful objects. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain sabiqin as those who escape God's decree. All conclude that God does not wrong anyone, and that people wronged themselves through disbelief and sin.

This verse states that God seized each of the peoples mentioned for their sin, and that each received a distinct punishment. Most commentators understand the hasib, a storm carrying pebbles or gravel, as the punishment of the people of Lot, though Ibn 'Atiyya suggests that the people of 'Ad may also be included, since their wind pelted them with harmful things. The cry (al-sayha) struck Thamud, and Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada add the people of Madyan, while al-Tabari holds that both nations were seized by the cry. The sinking into the earth applies to Qarun by general agreement, and drowning applies to the people of Noah and to Pharaoh and his people, though al-Tabari argues that the verse refers to both groups. All agree that God did not wrong them; rather they wronged themselves through disbelief and sin. al-Razi offers another reading in which the punishments correspond to the four elements, while al-Zamakhshari suggests that an angel may have been the one hurling stones. Ibn Juzayy, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi connect the punishments to divine justice, which strikes in proportion to the offence. Ibn Kathir notes that the passage recalls punishments already mentioned in the surah. The shared conclusion is that each people received a penalty suited to its wrongdoing, and that the real injustice was committed against themselves.

This verse offers a comparison: those who take protectors besides Allah, namely idols from which they hope for help and benefit, are like the spider that makes a house for itself. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, the comparison means these deities benefit neither their worshippers nor protect them from harm, just as the spider's web shields it neither from heat nor cold. These same commentators, with Ibn Abbas and Qatada, see in the passage a picture of the powerlessness of the polytheist and of his god. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that the comparison concerns the trust placed in what is taken as a support in religion, and they note that the spider's web is the weakest of houses. The phrase 'if they only knew' is read in two ways: for al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi, it means that if they knew how feeble their situation is, they would not worship others than Allah; for Ibn Atiyya, it means that they would recognise this as their own likeness. Al-Razi lists several reasons for choosing this example, such as the fact that the spider's web offers no real shelter, and Ibn Ashur sees the image as one of the Qur'an's original figures of speech. Commentators also cite reports about the spider, with varying reliability. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir mention views on not killing spiders, while others call it a devil to be slain; the commentators do not settle these views. Finally, the rest of the passage, which says Allah knows what they call upon and that only those with knowledge grasp these parables, is read by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi as an invitation to reflect on the Qur'anic parables.

This verse states that God knows fully what those who associate partners with Him invoke besides Him, and that these idols and deities possess nothing, while He alone is the Mighty, the Wise. Readers differ over the verb tad'una, a second-person reading followed by most readers and preferred by al-Tabari because it addresses living people, while Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ya'qub read it in the third person, which Abu 'Ubayd chose because the preceding verses speak of earlier nations. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take ma as a relative pronoun, so the sense is that God knows how worthless what they worship is. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan also explain that if ma is read as an interrogative or negative particle, the phrase becomes a confirmation of the parable and a rebuke to those who worship what is nothing, or a warning. Commentators on the next verse explain that the parables are offered to people to bring abstract truths close to understanding, and that only those who know God and His signs grasp their meaning. Ibn Kathir cites a report about Amr ibn al-As memorising a thousand parables, while others note weaknesses in the chains. Several commentators, including al-Razi and Ibn Ashur, observe that closing the verse with might and wisdom suits the idolaters' hope for help from their idols better than closing with knowledge.

The commentators explain that God strikes parables for people to bring distant meanings closer to their understanding, and that only those who grasp their beauty and benefit, namely the knowers of God and His signs, truly comprehend them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Jaza'iri take the reference to be to the Quran's parables in general, including the spider parable of the preceding verse about those who take protectors besides God. Most agree that 'reason' here means understanding and discernment, and that the knower is one who recognizes God and reflects on His signs. Some cite a hadith from Jabir defining the knower as one who understands from God and acts in obedience to Him, but Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Hajar considered this tradition weak or fabricated, so it cannot bear the weight of argument. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi report that the foolish of Quraysh mocked God's use of the fly and the spider as examples, and the verse replies that only the knowledgeable grasp their worth. Al-Razi distinguishes intuitive intelligence, which belongs to the rational person, from the precise reflective understanding of the scholar, and al-Nasafi concludes from this that knowledge is superior to intellect alone. Ibn Ashur reads the verse as a rebuke to those who neglect to reflect on the parables and ridicule them. Readings of the verb 'they call upon' differ between the second and third person, which changes whether the address is to the polytheists or to the earlier nations.

This verse states that God created the heavens and the earth with truth, meaning with justice and wisdom, not in vain or as play, and that this is a clear sign of His power and oneness. The commentators agree that the word haqq refers to the perfection of the creation and a sound purpose: God made them dwellings for His servants and a lesson for those who reflect. The specific mention of believers is explained by most as meaning that they are the ones who benefit from these signs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya link this verse to what precedes it, since the orderly creation of the world shows that worshipping idols is empty. Al-Razi sees in it a consolation for the believers when others refuse faith: their disbelief cannot cast doubt on the truth of their religion. Al-Zamakhshari explains haqq as the correct purpose, a phrase that Ibn al-Munayyir criticised as unsuitable. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi offer another reading in which haqq means God's speech and power. Several commentators stress that the believer perceives proofs in creation that others do not. Ibn 'Ashur notes that naming only believers implies that the others did not grasp this proof. Taken together, the commentaries invite the reader to reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to recite what has been revealed to him of the Book and to establish the prayer. The commentators explain that prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing, but they differ on the meaning of this restraint. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, followed by many others, hold that prayer keeps its performer back through the fear and remembrance of God it produces, and that whoever is not restrained by his prayer gains only greater distance from God. Al-Hasan and Qatada went further, saying such a prayer becomes a burden upon its performer. Others, such as Ibn 'Awn, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman and Ibn Jurayj, understood that prayer restrains as long as one is within it. Ibn 'Atiyya held that prayer is a cause leading to abstention from sin, through humility and awareness of standing before God. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Zayd took the verse to mean the call to good, while Ibn 'Umar understood the prayer here as the Qur'an recited in it.

As for the words "and the remembrance of God is greater", two readings are prominent. The first, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Salman, Abu al-Darda', Mujahid and 'Ikrima, and preferred by al-Tabari, is that God's remembrance of His servant is greater than the servant's remembrance of Him. The second, reported from Qatada and Ibn Zayd, is that the remembrance of God surpasses every act of worship. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur read it as a general restraint from evil, since remembering God prevents disobedience both within prayer and outside it. Some scholars combined the two readings, the phrase being capable of both meanings.

Several note that the command to recite includes acting upon the Qur'an's prescriptions, and that the address to the Prophet extends to his community unless a text limits it. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate the account of the young Ansari who kept committing sins and then repented after it was said that his prayer would restrain him, while noting that several chains of transmission for these reports are weak or stop at the Companions.

This verse commands the believers to argue with the People of the Book only in the best manner, meaning with gentle speech, by inviting them to God and drawing their attention to His proofs. The commentators agree that the exception, "except those of them who have done wrong", refers to those who were unjust in their rejection and obstinacy, but they differ on the details. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Tabari, and Ibn al-Jawzi, among others, understand these to be enemies at war who refused to pay the poll tax and fought the Muslims, whom one must confront with the sword until they embrace Islam or pay the tax. Ibn Zayd takes them to be those who persist in disbelief after the proof has been established. Others take them to be those who went to excess in aggression, who ascribed a son or partner to God, or who harmed the Prophet. On abrogation, Qatada and others hold that the verse was abrogated by the fighting verse in Surat al-Tawba, while al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd consider it firm, since God's rulings are abrogated only by clear evidence. The phrase "Say: we believe in what has been revealed to us and to you" is, for many, a form of argument in the best manner. It means that one should neither confirm nor deny what the People of the Book say when their truth cannot be known, as the hadith transmitted by Abu Hurayra states. The words "our God and your God is one" affirm monotheism and imply a rebuke of those who took their rabbis and monks as lords besides God. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the verse sets a principle for debate: begin with what both sides agree upon before turning to points of disagreement.

This verse states that the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ just as the scriptures were revealed to the messengers before him, and that those given the Book believe in it, as do some of the Meccans. Only the disbelievers deny Allah's signs once they have appeared. The commentators agree that denial comes only after knowledge, as Qatada says. They differ, however, on who is meant. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take the first group to be Abdullah ibn Salam and the believers among the People of the Book, and the second group to be the Arabs of Mecca. Al-Razi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan understand the People of the Book contemporary with the Prophet, and al-Razi even considers the prophets themselves. Al-Zamakhshari suggests that the deniers may be Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions. Ibn Kathir and others then note that the Prophet could neither read nor write, which they present as evidence of his truthfulness. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Kathir also record the debate over whether the Prophet ever wrote, which Ibn Kathir and most exegetes attribute to a command given rather than to a personal act. Al-Shawkani and al-Sha'rawi stress that the Qur'an is both the revelation and the sign that proves it.

This verse states that the Prophet ﷺ did not read any book or write with his right hand before the Qur'an was revealed, and that he was known among his people as unlettered. Had he been able to read and write, the wrongdoers would have had grounds for doubt, saying he had learned or copied the Qur'an from earlier writings. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others explain it this way, and Ibn Kathir notes that his unlettered status is also described in the earlier scriptures. Al-Tabari and Mujahid report that the People of the Book found in their texts that the Prophet would neither write nor read, and the verse came to confirm this.

Commentators differ on who the "wrongdoers" (al-mubtilun) are. Mujahid identifies them as the Quraysh polytheists, Qatada as the Arab polytheists or the People of the Book depending on the context, Muqatil as the Jews, and al-Suddi as the Jews who rejected the message. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi consider them to be both People of the Book and Meccan polytheists in different respects.

Regarding the phrase "Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those given knowledge," al-Hasan and al-Tabari take it to mean the Qur'an memorized in the hearts of believers, while Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatada take it to mean the description of the unlettered Prophet found in the scriptures of the People of the Book. Ibn Kathir considers the second meaning more apparent. Some exegetes add that his unlettered state is itself evidence of the Qur'an's divine origin.

On whether the Prophet wrote with his own hand at Hudaybiyya, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that al-Baji and others held that he did write, while most scholars interpreted the reports to mean he ordered someone to write, and several jurists rejected al-Baji's view strongly. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that even if he could write, this would not contradict the miraculous nature of the Qur'an.

This verse says that these are clear signs fixed in the hearts of those who have been given knowledge, and that only wrongdoers deny them. The commentators differ on what "it" refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi take it mainly to mean the Prophet ﷺ, whose description is found in the earlier scriptures and recognised by the learned among the People of the Book; al-Tabari cites the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, "bal hiya ayat bayyinat", in support. Al-Hasan, al-Tabari in another report, and al-Qurtubi take it to mean the Qur'an, with "those given knowledge" being the believers who memorised it; al-Hasan notes that this community was given memorisation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi stress that the preservation of the Qur'an in hearts is a feature that sets it apart from earlier books, which were read only from manuscripts. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and that "the hearts of those given knowledge" means, by way of honour, the heart of the Prophet ﷺ, or possibly those of his companions and the Muslim memorisers.

As for "none deny Our signs except the wrongdoers", most commentators understand it as people who reject signs that have become clear. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Mawardi identify them as polytheists, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi as disbelievers, while Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn Sa'di describe them as arrogant and stubborn people who know the truth and turn away from it. Ibn Sa'di adds that one who denies these signs is either ignorant or knows the truth yet opposes it out of enmity.

Several commentators, including al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir, also discuss whether the Prophet ﷺ could write. Ibn Kathir reports that most scholars deny that he ever wrote, and read the contrary reports as an order to write.

This verse reports the objection of the Meccan disbelievers, who asked why a sign had not been sent down to the Prophet ﷺ from his Lord, like the she-camel given to Salih or the table spread for Jesus. God tells him to reply that signs belong to Him alone, who sends them as He wills, and that his task is only to warn and to make things clear. Commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud agree that the verse rejects demands for chosen miracles, leaving the decision to God alone and assigning the Prophet the role of warner. Most add that God answered them with the Qur'an itself, a lasting sign recited to people in every age and place, a mercy and reminder for believers, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi state. The readings differ between the singular 'aya', read by Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, and the plural 'ayat', read by the others, which Abu 'Ubayd preferred. Ibn Kathir explains that God knows these askers seek only to test and provoke, so He does not grant them. Al-Razi holds that prophethood does not require a requested miracle, and that God sends a sign if He wills. A tradition links the revelation to people who brought the Prophet writings containing some Jewish statements, and he said, 'Enough folly for a people to turn away from what their prophet brought.' Ibn 'Ashur notes that such demands for visible wonders reflect the coarseness of these people, while al-Zamakhshari stresses that the Qur'an suffices in place of every requested sign. The passage closes with God's testimony for His messenger and the ruin of those who prefer falsehood to truth.

The commentators explain that the verse answers those among the Quraysh who demanded signs like those given to earlier prophets. The Qur'an itself is a lasting sign, recited in every age and place, a mercy and a reminder for those who believe, meaning those who seek the truth without obstinacy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya link the verse to the Quraysh, while al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also mention that it may address the People of the Book, who found the Prophet's description in their scriptures. Most cite a report from Yahya ibn Ja'da about pages containing parts of the Torah, which the Prophet disapproved of; al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya treat this report with some reserve, and Ibn 'Atiyya prefers the broader reading. Al-Razi argues that the Qur'an is a more complete proof than earlier miracles, since it endures and reaches every land, and that its mercy lies in distinguishing the true prophet from the impostor. Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi see it as healing and guidance for those who receive it with a sound heart. Al-Zamakhshari reads the question as a rebuke for not being content with the Qur'an, and Ibn 'Ashur lists five features that set it above other miracles. All agree that God's testimony suffices, and that the true losers are those who believed in falsehood and disbelieved in God.

God commands His Prophet ﷺ to tell the pagans who demanded a striking sign that God is sufficient as a witness between him and them, for He knows what is in the heavens and the earth, and knows his condition and theirs. The commentators understand this testimony in different ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it as God's witness to the Prophet's truthfulness, confirmed by the miracles and by the Book He sent down; al-Mawardi reads it as a witness to sincerity and transmission, with God also attesting to their denial. For the preceding verse, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir explain that the Qur'an itself suffices as a sign, a lasting proof recited at every time and place, a mercy and a reminder for believers. Several report the occasion of revelation: some Muslims brought the Prophet writings containing Jewish sayings, and he rejected them. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and most exegetes mention this account, though not all give it weight. As for 'those who believe in falsehood', most understand idolaters who worship other than God; al-Tabari relates it to associating partners, Yahya ibn Sallam to Iblis, Muqatil to the worship of Satan. Al-Razi argues that whatever is other than God is perishing and therefore vain. The loss is described by al-Mawardi as ruin of their own souls, and by others as the loss of Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud note that the wording is gentle and avoids direct accusation.

God tells us that the disbelievers were urging the Prophet ﷺ to bring the punishment, mocking him and denying him, as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith did when he said, "Rain down stones upon us from heaven." God did not hasten it, because He had set for it a known term that can neither be advanced nor delayed; were it not for that term, the punishment would have come at once. He then affirms that it will surely come upon them suddenly, while they are heedless and do not perceive its time. The commentators agree that the cause of their haste was denial and mockery, but they differ on the appointed term. Ibn Jubayr, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir take it to be the Day of Resurrection; al-Dahhak takes it to be the span of their lives; Yahya ibn Sallam takes it to be the first blast of the trumpet; and many, including Ibn 'Abbas and al-Nasafi, take it to be the Day of Badr or the time of their deaths at their appointed terms. As for the punishment that comes suddenly, some understand it as the punishment of this world, such as the battle of Badr, while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir understand it as the punishment of the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir reports that Jahannam encompasses the disbelievers, and he cites an interpretation he judges strange, that Jahannam is the sea. Readers differ between "yaqulu" and "naqulu", a difference that hardly alters the meaning. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a reply to their objections, containing a warning of two punishments, one soon and a greater one in Hell. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that people will not perceive the coming punishment until its appointed time.

This verse concerns the disbelievers who urged the Prophet ﷺ to bring about the punishment he had warned them of, mocking him and challenging him. The commentators explain that the punishment will certainly reach them, and that Hell already surrounds them and awaits them. There is broad agreement that the disbelievers mentioned are the very ones who demand the punishment, and that being encompassed means that none of them will escape. Ibn Kathir and others take this to mean that Hell will gather all of them without exception. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi allow that the encompassing may be future, or present, since the disbelief and sins that lead to Hell already surround them. As for the "appointed term" mentioned just before, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr understand it as the Day of Resurrection, Qatada as the span of life until death and then until resurrection, Yahya ibn Sallam as the first blast of the trumpet, al-Dahhak as the length of their lives, and others as the Battle of Badr. Regarding Hell itself, Ikrima takes it to mean the sea, a view that Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir consider weak or strange, since most commentators understand the familiar fire. The readings differ on the verb "will say", whether in the third person or the first person plural, which determines whether the speaker is God, an angel charged with punishment, or a divine majesty. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di link this passage to the punishment of the Hereafter, from which none escapes, whether the worldly punishment is hastened for them or deferred.

This verse describes the Day of Judgement, when punishment will envelop the disbelievers from above them and from beneath their feet, and they will be told, as a rebuke: taste what you used to do. The commentators agree that Hell surrounds them and that punishment reaches them from every side, which intensifies it. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that this covering from above and below means the fire encircles them completely, and Ibn Kathir links it to other verses about layers of fire above and below. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur see the words addressed to the damned as a moral humiliation added to the physical torment. The verse belongs to a context in which the Quraysh challenged the Prophet to bring the punishment: al-Baghawi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report that this demand was mockery and denial, and that God delayed the punishment until an appointed term, which the commentators understand variously as the Day of Resurrection (Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr), the span of their lives (al-Dahhak) or the battle of Badr. On the reading, Nafi' and the Kufans read 'yaqulu' in the third person, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read 'naqulu' in the first person plural, which al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi take to refer to God or to an angel charged with the punishment. Al-Razi notes a gradation in the verse, since fire coming from above is not natural in this world. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the omission of the right and left sides serves brevity in a context of threat.

God addresses His believing servants who could no longer worship Him freely in Mecca: His earth is vast, so when worship is impossible in one land they should migrate to another and devote their worship to Him alone. The commentators broadly agree that the verse urges emigration from a land where faith is persecuted or hindered, and many link it to the weak Muslims of Mecca, as Muqatil and al-Kalbi report and as Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya repeat. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' say one must leave any land where sins are committed and cannot be changed, a view Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi attribute also to Malik. Mujahid reads it as a call to emigrate and fight, Abu al-'Aliya as a call to seek God's friends, and Ibn Zayd takes its address to be the Meccan believers. Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir instead takes the vastness to refer to God's mercy or provision, while al-Tabari prefers the emigration sense, since the words that follow, 'so worship Me alone,' support it. Several exegetes stress that death comes to everyone, so fear of it should not prevent migration, and that God provides for the emigrant just as He provides for animals that store nothing. A hadith cited by al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, that whoever flees with his religion from one land to another, even a span of earth, earns Paradise, appears in several of these works. On grammar, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss the role of the fa' and the fronting of the object, which they link to an implied condition.

This verse states that every soul will taste death and then be returned to God. The commentators read it in the context of the call to emigrate from a land of idolatry to a place where God can be worshipped: it reassures believers that death reaches everyone wherever they are. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir link it to the command to emigrate, while Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr speak of leaving places of disobedience. According to al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud, 'tasting' death means feeling its bitterness and distress. Al-Razi offers a subtler reading: one who clings to God rather than to himself escapes true death, which for believers is only a transition. Al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur stress the sense of return for judgment and reward. On recitation, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan record variants: the majority read 'turji'un' in the second person, while Abu Bakr, transmitting from Asim, reads it in the third person. The hadith cited by al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, linking the verse to the prohibition of hoarding food, is judged weak by al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani because it contradicts the established practice of the Prophet. The shared message is that death is inevitable and should therefore not deter from obedience.

This verse states that those who believe and do righteous deeds will be settled by God in lofty chambers in Paradise, beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever; an excellent reward for those who work. The commentators explain that it follows the call to the weak believers in Mecca to emigrate, and it encourages them with the promise of this reward. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari explain that the verb "nubawwi'annahum" means to settle or lodge them, while the reading with the letter thaʾ, "nathwiyannahum", means to make them dwell; they regard the two readings as close in meaning. The "ghuraf" are elevated chambers. All stress patience and trust in God as the essence of good; the patient are those who persevere in faith, emigration and the harm inflicted by the polytheists. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi observe that provision is not tied to a particular land: God feeds animals and those who emigrate. Al-Razi notes that the absence of any mention of something above the chambers signals their great height, unlike the punishment of the disbelievers, for whom fire is mentioned above them. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that "My earth is vast" may mean: emigrate from a land of wrongdoing, or that God's mercy and provision are vast, or that one should fight God's enemies. All remind that death comes to every soul, so it should not deter the believer from obedience. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani judge some reports about the occasion of the verse on the creature that does not carry its provision to be weak, but retain the common meaning: animals do not store food, and God provides for them.

The commentators explain that this verse (29:59) closes the description of those who believed and did righteous deeds: they are “those who persevered” through hardship, the hostility of the idolaters and exile, and who “put their trust in their Lord”, relying on Him alone. The passage belongs to an exhortation to the weak believers in Mecca to emigrate to God’s vast earth and not to let fear of death prevent them, since every soul will taste death. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan, agree that patience and trust in God gather all good, and that the reward mentioned is the upper chambers of Paradise. Their differences begin with the reading: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read “linathwiyannahum”, meaning “we will settle them”, while the others read “lanubawwi'annahum”, “we will lodge them”; al-Tabari holds that both readings have close meanings. They also differ on the phrase “My earth is vast”: Ibn Jubayr and Ata' take it as a call to leave a land of disobedience, Mujahid as a call to fight God’s enemies, Mutarrif as a reference to God’s mercy or provision, and Abu al-'Aliya as an invitation to seek God’s friends. On the next verse, “how many a creature does not carry its provision”, al-Hasan and Mujahid understand that such creatures do not store food, whereas Ibn Abbas restricts storing to humans, ants and mice. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani consider the reported occasion of revelation linked to hunger weak, and al-Qurtubi notes that the Prophet himself stored his family’s provision for a year.

The commentators explain that this verse follows the command to the believers in Mecca to emigrate, when they feared poverty and hunger in a land where they had no property or kin. God states that many creatures cannot carry their provision and do not store it for tomorrow, yet God provides for them, and He will provide for the believers too, for He hears their words and knows what their hearts hold. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the point to be that God takes responsibility for the sustenance of all creatures wherever they are. Nearly all agree that 'dabba' means any creature that crawls or walks on the earth, and that 'does not carry its provision' means it neither stores nor earns. Ibn 'Abbas and Sufyan are reported to have said that only humans, ants and mice store food, a view repeated by al-Zamakhshari and others. As for 'does not carry', some take it to mean weakness, others the lack of saving, and others the idea that God alone guarantees sustenance. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir connect the verse to emigration and consider saving incompatible with firm certainty; Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani cite a hadith of Ibn 'Umar on the matter but regard it as weak, since it conflicts with the established practice of the Prophet, who kept his family's yearly provision. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud read it as a comparison: the weak animal and the strong human alike receive their livelihood from God, who alone is its true cause.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that if he asked the polytheists who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they would certainly answer that God did it, and God marvels at their turning away from His oneness after acknowledging His lordship. Several commentators place the verse in a context of reassuring believers who feared poverty during emigration: the One who created the heavens and the earth is the One who provides for the weak creatures that store no provision, so they should not fear for their livelihood. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur agree that the verse establishes that the polytheists acknowledge the unity of lordship, and that their rejection of unity in worship is astonishing. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that acknowledging lordship entails acknowledging divinity, while al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud read the question "how are they turned away" as a rebuke and an expression of amazement. The commentators differ on the pronoun in "and restricts it for him": al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it as referring to the same person, whereas Abu Hayyan allows that it may refer to other people, some receiving abundance while others receive restriction. Most stress that wealth and poverty are a test and a divine wisdom, and do not by themselves indicate God's approval or displeasure, as al-Jaza'iri and Ibn 'Ashur note. Ibn Sa'di draws an extended argument from the verse against the worship of idols.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that God alone expands provision for whomever He wills among His servants and restricts it for whomever He wills, according to His knowledge of what suits each one, and that all of this flows from His wisdom and His all-encompassing knowledge. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, agree that both abundance and constraint are a test: wealth does not in itself indicate God's approval, nor poverty His anger, but each tests whether the servant gives thanks or is ungrateful, whether he endures or despairs. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya connect the verse to the call to emigrate, some believers having feared hardship, and recall that God provides even for the beasts. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the mention of knowledge opens subtle points about the completeness of divine will and wisdom, and that the pronoun 'him' may refer to one person who is sometimes expanded and sometimes restricted, or to another person; Abu Hayyan, al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur set out both readings. Ibn Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri stress that the verse establishes both the lordship and the sole right to worship, and denounces the inconsistency of polytheists who acknowledge God as creator and provider while associating others with Him. All agree that God knows all things, nothing about His servants or their interests escaping Him.

The commentators explain that God commands His Prophet ﷺ to ask the polytheists who sent down water from the sky and thereby revived the earth after its death. They will all answer that it is God, and the Prophet is then told to praise God for the proof that has been established against them, while most of them do not reason, meaning they fail to see the contradiction in acknowledging God's lordship while worshipping others beside Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur agree that the Meccan pagans acknowledged God as Creator, Provider and Giver of life, and that their refusal to associate others with Him follows from that acknowledgment. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the praise as thanks for the establishment of the argument, or for keeping the Prophet from such error, while al-Razi notes that it may be a parenthetical remark, or that it exposes their self-contradiction. Al-Biqa'i and Ibn Sa'di hold that the argument obliges them to affirm the oneness of divinity after affirming the oneness of lordship. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the praise covers all the preceding proofs and not only the argument from rain, and that 'most' means some believed while others persisted in obstinacy.

The commentators explain that this verse belittles the life of this world, describing it as mere amusement and play, a pleasure that distracts for a while and then vanishes, like children who play briefly and then disperse. The life of the Hereafter is the true and lasting life, without death. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas explain that al-hayawan means the everlasting life that has neither end nor death. Abu 'Ubayda, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba hold that hayawan and hayat have the same meaning, a view adopted by Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, argues that the pattern fa'alan adds a sense of movement and vitality, which intensifies the idea of a full life in the Hereafter. Al-Razi distinguishes play, which is attention given to falsehood, from amusement, which is turning away from truth. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse addresses both the wise and the common people. Ibn 'Uthaymin states that good deeds performed in this world belong to the Hereafter because their fruit appears there, so they are not mere play. The commentators agree that the conditional clause after 'if' has an implied answer: had they known, they would not have preferred the transient to the lasting. The context is a rebuke of polytheism and of the unbelievers' heedlessness of the Hereafter.

This verse describes people who, aboard a ship and seized by fear of drowning, call upon God alone with sincere devotion, and then, once delivered to dry land, return to associating others with Him. The commentators broadly agree that in distress these people recognise that only God can rescue them, which makes their return to polytheism all the more blameworthy. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi stress this contrast between the sincerity of the danger and the forgetfulness that follows deliverance. Al-Baghawi, quoting Ikrima, reports that the pre-Islamic Arabs would throw their idols into the sea when the storm rose, crying out, "O Lord, O Lord." Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi see irony in describing them as sincere worshippers, since their sincerity appears only in the trial. On the particle in "li-yakfuru", most read it as a particle of purpose, meaning that their return to idolatry ends in ingratitude for the rescue and in enjoying worldly life, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baghawi, and Ibn Atiyya take the lam as an imperative of warning, a reading supported by the sukun variant. Al-Razi observes that attachment to the world prevents the return to the monotheistic nature that people naturally have, which surfaces in hardship. Ibn Ashur adds that the Arabs travelled mainly by land and therefore feared the sea more.

This passage of Surat al-'Ankabut describes idolaters who, in fear at sea, call upon Allah alone with sincerity, but once saved and back on land return to polytheism. The commentators explain that "so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them" means denying the blessing of their deliverance. As for "and so that they may enjoy themselves", the reading with a kasra on the lam (purpose) and the reading with a sukun (imperative of threat) are discussed. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi prefer the sukun reading, which expresses threat and rebuke, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur accept both readings, sometimes calling the lam one of consequence rather than intent. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi present both interpretations. All agree that the closing words "they will soon know" carry a warning, and that the passage rebukes the contradiction between sincerity in danger and idolatry in ease. The following verses mention the secure sanctuary that protects the Quraysh while other Arabs are raided. Al-Tabari and Qatada see this as a favour that calls for gratitude, and the falsehood they believe in is idolatry. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Sa'di and Ibn Ashur note that the worldly life is mere play and amusement compared with the enduring abode of the Hereafter. The passage ends with the promise of guidance for those who strive for Allah, which al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi interpret in different ways, some as inner struggle and others as outward fighting.

This passage rebukes the Meccan polytheists for an inconsistency: when they board a ship and fear drowning, they call upon God alone with sincere devotion, but as soon as He brings them safely to land they return to associating others with Him. Commentators explain the phrase "so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them" as meaning that this return to idolatry amounts to denying the favour of their rescue. The reading "wa-liyatamatta'u" with a vocalised lam is taken by some as an imperative of threat, while the reading with a sukun lam is read as a purpose or consequence; al-Tabari prefers the threat reading as fitting the context, and many later exegetes agree. The next verse recalls the favour of a secure sanctuary: the tribes around Mecca raided one another, while its people lived in peace, so they ought to be grateful. Scholars differ on what the "falsehood" is: Qatada says it is associationism, Yahya ibn Salam says Iblis, and others say the idols. Likewise with "the blessing of God": Ibn Abbas takes it as well-being, others as Islam and the message of the Prophet, and others as the feeding and security granted to them. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari stress that a blessing so evident can only come from God, which makes denying it all the more serious. Finally, "those who strive for Us" is understood by most commentators as fighting the enemies of the faith, though some include the struggle against one's own soul and desires, or acting on what one knows; Ibn Kathir and others note that the wording is general and covers every striving in God's cause.

The plain meaning of the verse is that there is no one more wrongdoing than the one who fabricates a lie against God, such as by claiming He has a partner or a son, or by attributing to Him an order to commit an indecency, or who denies the truth when it has come to him, namely monotheism, the Qur'an, or the Prophet ﷺ, and that the abode of these disbelievers is Hell. The commentators explain that the question 'is there not' is an affirmation rather than a genuine question, as shown by the famous verse of Jarir that most of them cite. Most agree that the fabrication is ascribing a partner to God and the denial is rejecting the truth. They differ, however, on what 'the truth' refers to: al-Sudi and Ibn Shajara say monotheism, Yahya ibn Sallam says the Qur'an, Ibn Shajara also says the Prophet ﷺ, and al-Qurtubi holds that each view is included in the others. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the phrase 'when it came to them' rebukes their hasty rejection without reflection. For the next verse, the commentators agree that those who strive for God will be guided, but they differ on the meaning of striving. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand it as fighting enemies and defending the religion, al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Mubarak as struggling against the soul and its desires, and Abu Sulayman al-Darani as acting on what one knows. On guidance, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as steadfastness and increased guidance, while al-Sudi takes it as the path to Paradise. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi add that God is with the doers of good, with help in this world and reward in the next.

This verse states that those who strive for God, that is, who exert themselves seeking His pleasure, God will guide to His paths, and that God is with the good-doers through His support and help. The commentators largely agree that the word jihad here has a broad meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi first understand it as fighting the enemies of the faith to support God's religion. Al-Hasan al-Basri, Abu Sulayman al-Darani, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Qayyim include the struggle against the self, desires and Satan, which al-Hasan considers the greatest jihad. Ibn Abbas links it to obedience to God, and al-Zamakhshari extends it to any struggle against the soul, Satan and the enemies of religion. On the meaning of guidance, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand steadiness and success on the straight path, while al-Suddi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya take it as the way to Paradise. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, report that whoever acts on what he knows is granted knowledge he did not have. Al-Razi offers a philosophical reading in which guidance follows from reflection on God's signs. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the verse was revealed before armed fighting was made obligatory. As for God's being with them, most commentators understand it as help and support, and Ibn al-Jawzi specifies that those meant are the monotheists or the fighters.
